intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting power, and say how a change in speed or feed changes tool life and surface finish.
intro.whyItMatters: Machining sets the cost and the tolerance of most precision parts, and its calculations are simple once the units are kept straight.

recap.keyIdea: Cutting speed is pi x D x N / 1000, removal rate is v x f x d, power is that rate times specific energy, and tool life falls as speed to the power -1 / n.

blocks.text: The cutting speed of a turned bar is pi x D x N / 1000, and with the feed and depth it gives the removal rate v x f x d and, with the specific energy, the cutting power. Tool life falls as speed to the power -1 / n, so a 20 percent rise in speed roughly halves it, and the theoretical roughness f^2 / (32 r) depends on feed and nose radius alone.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson compares moulding, printing and machining by cost, and finds the volume at which tooling pays back.

lessons.title: Moulding, printing and cost per part

lead.text: In **injection moulding** plastic granules are melted and forced under high pressure into a closed steel mould, where the plastic cools and sets. The mould then opens and pins eject the part, and the cycle repeats, in a few seconds for small parts.

afterFigure.text: The injected plastic pushes on the walls of the cavity with a pressure of tens of megapascals, and the two halves of the mould would be forced apart if they were not held. The **clamp force** needed is the cavity pressure times the **projected area**, the area of the part seen in the direction in which the mould opens. At 50 MPa on 10,000 mm2, the force is 50 x 10,000 = 500,000 N, or 500 kN, since 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2.

diagram.alt: Three stages of injection moulding drawn as a cross-section: hot plastic injected into the closed mould while a clamp force holds the halves together, the plastic cooling and setting, and the mould opening to eject the part.
diagram.caption: The cycle repeats every few seconds to a minute. The clamp has to hold the mould shut against the pressure of the injected plastic.

reveal.text: Machines are sold by their clamp force in tonnes or kilonewtons, and the choice of machine follows from this calculation.

lead.text: Making a part by injection moulding costs two kinds of money. The mould, the **tooling**, is paid for once and can cost tens of thousands of dollars. After that each part costs only the plastic and the machine time, perhaps 1.50. Printing a part needs no tooling, but every part costs the same, say 12, whether it is the first or the thousandth.

afterFigure.text: So the total cost is the tooling plus the cost per part times the number of parts, and the average cost per part is the tooling divided by the number of parts plus the cost per part.

reveal.text: The comparison depends on the quantity, and the next screen finds the quantity at which the two totals are equal.

lead.text: Moulding and printing cost the same when 20,000 + 1.50 n = 12 n, where n is the number of parts. Collecting the terms gives 20,000 = (12 - 1.50) n, so the **break-even volume** is n = 20,000 / 10.50 = 1905 parts. Each moulded part saves 10.50 dollars against a printed one, and the tooling is paid back when those savings reach 20,000.

afterFigure.text: The first graph shows the two total costs, which cross at 1905 parts: below it the printed line is lower, and above it the moulded line is.

lead.text: For a handful of parts, printing or machining wins because they carry no tooling cost. For thousands or millions of parts, injection moulding wins, because the tooling is shared out so thinly that it hardly shows. In between, the answer depends on the cost of the tooling and on how much each process saves per part, which is just what the break-even volume measures.

afterFigure.text: The boundary moves with the numbers. A simple part with a cheap mould breaks even at a few hundred parts, and a complex part with a mould of several hundred thousand dollars may not do so until it passes a hundred thousand. Printing also allows shapes that no mould could release.

reveal.text: Break-even is proportional to the tooling cost, so one pricey quotation can move a project from moulding to printing.

lead.text: Moulded parts have to be released from a steel mould, so every wall that runs in the direction in which the mould opens is given a slight taper called **draft**, typically between half a degree and two degrees. Without it the walls rub along the mould, and the part sticks or scratches. Draft moves the face of a wall by height x tan(angle): a draft of 1 degree on a wall 40 mm tall moves the face by 40 x tan(1 degree) = 0.70 mm.

afterFigure.text: The wall thickness should also be even. A thick section cools more slowly than a thin one, by the same reasoning that gave a freezing time depending on the square of V / A in casting, so it shrinks later and pulls a dimple, a sink mark, into the surface, or warps the part. Designers hollow out thick regions and use ribs instead, so that every section cools at about the same rate.

diagram.alt: A moulded part in section. With no draft its walls are vertical and rub against the mould as it is ejected. With draft its walls lean slightly so that the part clears the mould at once. The lean in the drawing is exaggerated.
diagram.caption: A small taper on every wall that is parallel to the opening direction lets the part come out cleanly.

Such small shifts add up on a deep part, which must be allowed for in the dimensions of the design.

lessons.reviewLabel: Moulding, printing and cost per part
lessons.nextAction: Look at tolerances and how often a process stays inside them, with Cp and Cpk.

blocks.text: A mould for a small plastic part can cost 20,000 dollars, after which each moulded part costs about 1.50, while the same part can be printed for 12 dollars with no mould at all. For a handful of parts printing is plainly cheaper and for a million moulding is, so somewhere between the two the total costs must be equal.

That crossing point follows from one line of algebra, and the same calculation applies to any cost paid once before the first part is made, such as a die or a pattern, set against a cost paid on every part.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute an injection-moulding clamp force, find the volume at which tooling pays back, and say when each process fits.
intro.whyItMatters: Most manufacturing decisions come down to a fixed cost against a cost per part, and the break-even volume says where the choice changes.

recap.keyIdea: Clamp force is cavity pressure times projected area, and tooling pays back at the break-even volume, tooling cost divided by the saving per part.

blocks.text: The clamp must hold the mould against the cavity pressure over the projected area, which for 10,000 mm2 at 50 MPa is 500 kN. Moulding has a high cost paid at the start and a low cost per part, so it beats printing only beyond the break-even volume, tooling cost divided by the saving per part, which was 1905 parts for 20,000 dollars of tooling. Good moulded parts have draft on their walls and an even thickness.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks how many of the parts that a process makes will actually meet the tolerance.

lessons.title: Holding tolerance in production

lead.text: Machine the same diameter on a thousand parts and the measurements will differ slightly, in a pattern that is close to a normal distribution. It has a mean, which is where the process is aimed or has drifted to, and a standard deviation **sigma**, which is the typical distance from the mean. About 99.73 percent of the parts lie within 3 sigma of the mean, so the whole range of a process covers about 6 sigma. The drawing specifies a **tolerance**, with a **lower specification limit** (LSL) and an **upper specification limit** (USL), and a part is good if it lies between them.

afterFigure.text: A process with sigma = 0.01 mm has its limits 5 sigma from the mean, and almost nothing falls outside. A process with sigma = 0.02 mm has them only 2.5 sigma away, and about 1.2 percent of parts fall outside, shown in the warm colour. Note that the tolerance and sigma are different quantities: one is what the customer wants, the other is what the process does.

diagram.alt: Two bell curves of the diameter of machined parts, centred on 25.00 mm, with lower and upper specification limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. The narrow curve, with a standard deviation of 0.01 mm, sits almost wholly inside the limits. The wide curve, with 0.02 mm, spills over both limits.
diagram.caption: Both processes aim at 25.00 mm. The narrow one fits inside the limits and the wide one does not. Shaded in warm colour is the part of the output that falls outside the limits.

reveal.text: Four sigma is a long way out: about 32 parts in a million fall beyond it.

lead.text: Dividing the tolerance range by the spread of the process gives a single number, the **process capability index** Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 sigma). For limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm, the range is 0.10 mm, and with sigma = 0.01 mm the spread is 0.06 mm, so Cp = 0.10 / 0.06 = 1.67. A Cp of 1 means the spread of the process just fills the tolerance, with no margin at all, and a value above 1 means the spread fits inside with room to spare. Many customers ask for 1.33 or more.

afterFigure.text: Cp compares widths and nothing else. It does not say where the process is centred, and a process can be as narrow as one likes and still be aimed at the wrong place, so Cp alone cannot say whether the parts are good.

steps.headline: Find Cp for limits of 49.90 and 50.10 mm and a standard deviation of 0.03 mm.

workedSteps.text: The tolerance range is the upper limit less the lower limit.
The spread of the process is 6 sigma.
Divide the tolerance range by the spread.
The process capability index is

reveal.text: A tolerance that exactly equals the 6 sigma spread leaves no allowance for drift.

lead.text: Tool wear can move the mean of a process while leaving its spread unchanged.

reveal.text: Cp does not notice that the mean has moved. The next screen introduces an index that does.

lead.text: The index that accounts for centring is Cpk = (the distance from the mean to the nearer limit) / (3 sigma). With the mean at 25.02 mm and limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm, the nearer limit is the upper one, 0.03 mm away, and Cpk = 0.03 / (3 x 0.01) = 1.0. A Cpk of 1.0 puts the nearer limit 3 sigma from the mean, so about 0.135 percent of parts are beyond it, even though Cp is still 1.67.

afterFigure.text: Cpk can never be larger than Cp, and the two are equal only when the mean sits exactly at the middle of the tolerance range. The figure keeps the spread fixed and moves the mean: at 25.00 mm Cpk is 1.67, at 25.02 mm it is 1.0, and at 25.04 mm it is 0.33, where about 16 percent of parts are above the upper limit. The remedy for a low Cpk with a high Cp is to recentre the process, which costs far less than narrowing it.

diagram.alt: Three bell curves with standard deviation 0.01 mm and limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. Centred on 25.00 mm, the process makes almost every part in limits and has a Cpk of 1.67. With its mean at 25.02 mm, a small tail passes the upper limit and Cpk is 1.0. With its mean at 25.04 mm, about 16 percent of parts are above the upper limit and Cpk is 0.33.
diagram.caption: The spread is the same in all three views, and only the mean moves. Cpk falls as the mean approaches a limit, while Cp stays at 1.67.

steps.headline: Find Cpk for a process with mean 24.985 mm and sigma 0.01 mm, with limits 24.95 and 25.05 mm.

workedSteps.text: The upper limit is 25.05 - 24.985 = 0.065 mm from the mean, and the lower limit is 24.985 - 24.95 = 0.035 mm away.
Cpk is the distance to the nearer limit divided by 3 sigma.

reveal.text: Recentring recovers all of the capability that the spread allows, since Cpk rises to meet Cp.

lead.text: The share of parts beyond the nearer limit follows from Cpk, if the distribution is normal. At Cpk = 1.0 about 0.135 percent, or 1350 parts per million, lie beyond it. At 1.33 the figure is about 32 parts per million, and at 1.67 it is about 0.3. A centred process with Cp = 1.0 puts 0.27 percent beyond the two limits together, which is twice the single tail.

afterFigure.text: Two warnings apply. A high Cp does not guarantee good parts, as the drifted process showed. And measuring more parts does not improve a process: the capability is a property of the process, and a larger sample only gives a better estimate of it. To raise Cpk, the spread must be narrowed or the mean recentred, by better machines, better fixtures, better tools or tighter control.

blocks.text: A shaft is drawn as 25.00 mm in diameter with a tolerance of 0.05 mm either way. Turn a thousand of them and no two will have exactly the same diameter, because tool wear, temperature and the material itself all vary a little from part to part. The question for production is whether almost all of the thousand will fall between 24.95 and 25.05 mm, and the answer depends on two things, how wide the spread of the process is and where it is centred.

diagram.alt: Two bell curves of the diameter of machined parts, centred on 25.00 mm, with lower and upper specification limits at 24.95 and 25.05 mm. The narrow curve, with a standard deviation of 0.01 mm, sits almost wholly inside the limits. The wide curve, with 0.02 mm, spills over both limits.
diagram.caption: Both processes aim at 25.00 mm. The narrow one fits inside the limits and the wide one does not. Shaded in warm colour is the part of the output that falls outside the limits.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute Cp and Cpk from a tolerance, a mean and a standard deviation, and say whether a process meets its tolerance.
intro.whyItMatters: A tolerance is only a promise if the process can keep it, and two numbers say whether it can.

recap.keyIdea: Cp is the tolerance range divided by 6 sigma, Cpk uses the distance from the mean to the nearer limit divided by 3 sigma, and Cpk is never larger than Cp.

blocks.text: A process meets a tolerance when its spread fits inside it and its mean is near the middle. Cp, the tolerance range divided by 6 sigma, measures the fit, and Cpk, the nearer limit's distance from the mean divided by 3 sigma, also measures the centring, so a process with Cp = 1.67 and a mean at 25.02 mm has Cpk = 1.0, and about 0.135 percent of its parts are beyond the nearer limit.

lessons.title: Choosing a material and a process

reveal.text: A beam that is weaker in stiffness has to be made bulkier to compensate, and the next screens show by how much.

lead.text: Selection begins with three questions. What must the part do, which is its **function**; what limits it, which are its **constraints**; and what should be as small as possible or as large as possible, which is its **objective**. Take a beam of a given length that must have a given stiffness S, with a mass that is to be as low as possible. The stiffness of a beam of square section with side b is proportional to E x b^4, so for a fixed S the side must be b proportional to 1 / E^(1/4). The mass is proportional to density x b^2, and putting in b gives a mass proportional to density / sqrt(E).

afterFigure.text: The lightest beam is therefore the one with the largest **performance index** sqrt(E) / density. This is not E alone, and not density alone: a stiffer material allows a smaller section, but only in proportion to the fourth root.

diagram.alt: Two square beam cross-sections drawn to scale, for beams of the same length and stiffness. The steel section has a side of 1.00 and the aluminium section a side of 1.32, which is 1.73 times the area, but aluminium is 0.34 times as dense, so the aluminium beam is lighter.
diagram.caption: To match a steel beam's stiffness, an aluminium beam must be larger, yet it still weighs less. The sizes are drawn to scale.

reveal.text: The index is a number for comparing, with no units that matter, since only its ranking is used.

lead.text: Calculating the index for common materials, with E in GPa and the density in g/cm3, gives steel 1.85, titanium 2.39, aluminium 3.10, pine 6.32 and a carbon-fibre composite 6.45. The mass of a beam with the same stiffness is proportional to the reciprocal of the index, so relative to steel an aluminium beam weighs 1.85 / 3.10 = 0.60, a titanium beam 0.77, and beams of pine or composite about 0.29. The aluminium beam saves 40 percent, not the 66 percent that its density alone suggests.

afterFigure.text: Two details are worth noticing. The metals are close together, so choosing between them depends on other properties, while the composite and the wood are much better because they combine a high stiffness with a low density. And the ranking changes with the function: a tie rod in tension has the index E / density, and on that measure steel and aluminium are almost equal.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts for steel, titanium, aluminium, pine and carbon-fibre composite: the performance index square root of E over density, and the mass of an equal-stiffness beam relative to steel. Carbon-fibre composite and pine are best, aluminium next, and steel is worst.
diagram.caption: A high index means a light beam for a given stiffness. The mass chart is the same ranking turned into a weight.

lead.text: Different functions give different indices: a beam that must be stiff gives sqrt(E) / density, a tie rod gives E / density, and a beam that must be strong instead of stiff gives an index with the yield strength. Used on the wrong job, the ranking can be wrong. A second limit is that the index looks at one objective, and a real part also has a cost, a corrosion environment and a way of being made.

afterFigure.text: Aluminium rivets in a steel plate, an example from the corrosion lesson, would rank well on mass and fail in salt spray, because the galvanic cell makes the aluminium the anode. Cost may rule out carbon fibre, and wood suffers in wet conditions. The usual method is to rank by the index, then to screen the leading materials against these other limits, and to take the best that survives.

reveal.text: The best material depends on the job, and aluminium, a clear winner for a beam, gives no saving on a tie rod.

lead.text: A process is chosen by what it can make. The **shape** rules some processes out: a hollow shape suits casting or moulding, a flat plate suits forming, a prismatic part with fine detail suits machining. The **volume** decides between processes with different tooling costs, as the break-even volume showed, so a few parts are printed or machined and thousands are cast or moulded. The **material** rules others out, because a thermoplastic is moulded and a carbon-fibre composite is **laid up**, built from layers of fibre sheet wetted with resin, and neither is cast.

afterFigure.text: Material and process therefore cannot be chosen separately. A beam in carbon-fibre composite needs a layup process and a certain shape, a die casting needs a metal that melts at a temperature the die can stand, and a high volume of small parts may force a change of material to suit a mould.

diagram.alt: Three cards matching a process to the job: by the shape, by the number of parts, and by the material.
diagram.caption: Shape, volume and material each rule some processes out. The choice is made by looking at all three.

blocks.text: Aluminium is about a third as dense as steel, which makes it look like the obvious choice for a light beam, but it is also only a third as stiff. An aluminium beam made to bend no more than a steel one of the same length therefore needs a larger cross-section, and whether it still comes out lighter, and by how much, depends on how quickly the mass grows as the section is enlarged.
Questions of this kind are settled with a single number for each material, worked out from the algebra of what the part has to do, which ranks every material for that one job.

intro.whyItMatters: Choosing the material and the process together is the last step from understanding materials to making things.

recap.keyIdea: A performance index, such as sqrt(E) / density for a stiff light beam, ranks materials for one job, and the process must be matched to the shape, the volume and the material.

blocks.text: For a beam of fixed stiffness the mass varies as density / sqrt(E), so materials are ranked by sqrt(E) / density: 1.85 for steel, 3.10 for aluminium, 6.45 for a carbon-fibre composite and 6.32 for pine, which makes an aluminium beam 0.60 of the mass of a steel one. The ranking holds for one function only, so cost, corrosion and the process have to be checked, and the process follows from shape, volume and material.

questions.prompt: A steel bar (E = 210 GPa) carries a stress of 105 MPa, within its elastic range. What is its strain, in percent?
hints: In the elastic range, strain is stress divided by the modulus E.
Convert E to MPa first: 210 GPa is 210,000 MPa.
Divide 105 by 210,000, then multiply by 100 to get a percent.
questions.onCorrect: Strain is 0.0005, so a 1 m length stretches by only 0.5 mm. Steel is stiff because E is large.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strain as a plain ratio. The question asks for percent, so multiply by 100.
That divides 105 by 210 without converting GPa to MPa. 210 GPa is 210,000 MPa.

questions.prompt: The same steel yields at 250 MPa. It is pulled to 300 MPa and the load is then removed completely. What happens to the bar?
hints: Compare 300 MPa with the yield strength of 250 MPa.
Think about whether the stretch beyond yield is recovered.

acceptedIdeas: It stays slightly longer than before.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stays slightly longer than before.

questions.onCorrect: Unloading follows a line parallel to the elastic one, so the plastic part of the stretch stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Steel is elastic only up to its yield strength. Beyond 250 MPa part of the stretch is permanent.
Removing load cannot break the bar. It follows a line parallel to the elastic one down to zero stress.

choices.label: It returns exactly to its original length, because steel is elastic.
It breaks as the load is removed.
It stays slightly longer than before.

Using the 0.2 percent offset method, at which stress does the alloy yield?
hints: At each stress the offset line sits 0.2 percent of strain to the right of the elastic line. Work out the elastic strain, stress divided by E, at a stress you want to test.
The yield strength is the stress where the measured strain first reaches the elastic strain plus 0.2 percent.
Compare the measured strain with that sum at 280 MPa and at 320 MPa. The curve is left of the offset line at one of them and right of it at the other.

acceptedIdeas: 300 MPa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 300 MPa

questions.onCorrect: At 300 MPa the offset line is at 0.629 percent strain and the curve is at 0.630 percent, so they cross there. At lower stresses the curve lies left of the offset line, and at higher stresses it lies to the right.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress where the total strain reaches 0.2 percent, and the bar is still on its elastic line there, so it springs back completely. The offset line is the elastic line moved 0.2 percent to the right, and the yield strength is where the curve meets it.

The curve has only just begun to leave the elastic line at 250 MPa, with a strain of 0.362 percent against 0.357 percent. The offset line is 0.2 percent to the right of the elastic line, and the curve does not reach it until a higher stress.

At 320 MPa the strain of 0.900 percent is already well past the offset line, which sits at 0.657 percent there. The yield strength is the stress where curve and offset line agree, which happens before 320 MPa.

questions.prompt: The 10 mm bar fractures with a neck diameter of 8 mm. Using A0 = 78.54 mm2 and Af = 50.27 mm2, what is the reduction in area, in percent to one decimal place?
hints: Reduction in area is the lost area divided by the original area.
Subtract 50.27 from 78.54 first.
Divide that difference by 78.54 and multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The neck lost 36 percent of the original area, a plain sign of ductile behaviour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final area as a share of the original. The reduction is what was lost.
That is the lost area in mm2. Divide it by the original area and express it as a percent.

questions.prompt: A crash bracket has to absorb as much energy as it can by deforming before it breaks. Steel A has a yield strength of 1,100 MPa, a tensile strength of 1,200 MPa and fractures at a strain of 0.03. Steel B has a yield strength of 250 MPa, a tensile strength of 400 MPa and fractures at a strain of 0.28. Treat each curve as a flat line at the average of its yield and tensile strengths, out to fracture. Which steel suits the bracket?
hints: The energy a material absorbs before it breaks, for each cubic metre, is the area under its stress-strain curve.
With a flat curve the area is the height times the width: the average stress times the fracture strain.

acceptedIdeas: Steel B, which absorbs about 91 MJ/m3 against 35 MJ/m3 for steel A
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Steel B, which absorbs about 91 MJ/m3 against 35 MJ/m3 for steel A

questions.onCorrect: Steel B absorbs 325 x 0.28 = 91 MJ/m3 and steel A only 1,150 x 0.03 = 34.5 MJ/m3. Toughness depends on how far a steel can deform as well as on the stress it carries.

misconceptions.feedback: Strength is the height of the curve, and the bracket needs the area under it. Steel A reaches a high stress but breaks at a strain of 0.03, so its area is about 1,150 x 0.03 = 34.5 MJ/m3.
Stiffness is the slope of the elastic line, and it says nothing about the energy absorbed up to fracture. That energy is the area under the whole curve, and the two areas differ by a factor of 2.6.

questions.onCorrect: Water cooling catches the carbon in the iron lattice before it can move into layers, and the strained structure that results, martensite, blocks dislocations so well that the steel is very hard and brittle. The furnace-cooled bar is pearlite, which a file can cut.

misconceptions.feedback: Slow cooling gives layers of ferrite and cementite because carbon has time to move into them. Plunging the bar into water leaves no time for that, so layers do not form.
The carbon stays in the steel. Ferrite is soft and ductile, which does not fit a bar that skids a file and chips when it is dropped.

choices.label: Martensite, with carbon trapped in a strained lattice that blocks dislocations
Ferrite, because the water carried the carbon out of the steel and left it soft
Pearlite, with finer layers than in the first bar, formed by the fast cooling

questions.prompt: A point count on a micrograph of a steel cooled slowly to just below 727 C shows that half of the area is pearlite and the other half is plain ferrite. Roughly what carbon content does the steel have, in weight percent to two decimal places?
hints: The pearlite share of a slowly cooled steel is the fraction that the lever rule gives, with the ferrite end of the bar at 0.022 percent and the pearlite end at 0.76 percent.
Set that fraction equal to 0.50 and solve for the carbon content C.
Multiply 0.50 by the length of the whole bar, 0.738, and add the ferrite end, 0.022.
questions.onCorrect: About 0.39 percent carbon, which is near the middle of the bar between 0.022 and 0.76.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the 0.022 at the ferrite end, which has to be added back.
That is the midpoint of 0 and 0.76. The bar starts at 0.022, not 0.

questions.prompt: A 0.30 percent carbon steel is cooled slowly to just below 727 C. What fraction of it is pearlite, to three decimal places?
hints: The arm on the ferrite side is 0.30 - 0.022.
The whole bar is 0.738 long.
Divide the arm by the whole bar.
questions.onCorrect: Roughly 38 percent pearlite, with the other 62 percent as soft proeutectoid ferrite.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of ferrite. Pearlite uses the arm on the ferrite side.
That divides the carbon content, 0.30, by 0.76. The arm and the whole bar both start at 0.022.

questions.prompt: A 0.40 percent carbon steel is cooled slowly from 900 C to room temperature. In what order do these things happen?
hints: Ferrite can hold very little carbon, so the first ferrite that forms leaves the carbon in the austenite around it.
The leftover austenite can turn into layers only when its carbon content reaches the eutectoid composition.
questions.onCorrect: Each step needs the one before it. The ferrite that forms first enriches the leftover austenite, and only when that austenite reaches 0.76 percent carbon at 727 C does it turn into pearlite.

items: The steel is austenite, a single uniform solid
Proeutectoid ferrite starts to form as the steel cools below the sloping line
The remaining austenite grows richer in carbon until it holds 0.76 percent at 727 C
The remaining austenite turns to layers of ferrite and cementite

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steel is all austenite at 900 C, ferrite forms as it cools past the sloping line, the leftover austenite is enriched to 0.76 percent carbon at 727 C, and that austenite then turns to pearlite.

questions.prompt: A chef's knife is quenched and must stay very hard at the edge, with only some of the brittleness removed. Which treatment fits?
hints: Which tempering temperature keeps the hardness closer to the as-quenched value?
Tempering trades hardness for toughness, and the higher the temperature, the more it trades. Decide how much trade the edge can afford.

acceptedIdeas: Temper it at 200 C
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Temper it at 200 C

questions.onCorrect: At 200 C the hardness stays close to its quenched value and a little of the brittleness goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Tempering at 500 C gives a tough but noticeably softer steel, which would not hold a sharp edge.
Steel as quenched is hard but brittle, and a knife in that state would chip.
Annealing makes steel soft and would undo the hardening.

choices.label: Temper it at 500 C
Anneal it
Temper it at 200 C
Leave it as quenched

questions.prompt: The handle of a cooking pot has to keep its shape however hot the pot gets in use, and it will never be melted down and remoulded. Which class of polymer suits it, and why?
hints: Ask what has to happen between the chains for a polymer to soften when it is warmed.
One class has its chains tied to each other, and the other has them held only by weak attractions.

acceptedIdeas: A thermoset, because covalent cross-links stop its chains sliding apart when it is heated
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A thermoset, because covalent cross-links stop its chains sliding apart when it is heated

questions.onCorrect: A thermoset's chains are tied into one network by cross-links, so heating cannot let them slide, and the handle stays solid until it is hot enough to decompose.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a thermoplastic's strength for recycling and remoulding, and it is the wrong property here. Warmed, its chains slide past each other and the handle would soften and sag.
The covalent bonds along the chains do not stop the chains sliding past each other. In a thermoplastic only weak secondary bonds hold the chains together, and heat overcomes them.
Both have covalent chains, but only a thermoset ties the chains to each other with cross-links, and that network is what keeps its shape until it decomposes.

choices.label: A thermoplastic, because its chains can be melted and set again
A thermoset, because covalent cross-links stop its chains sliding apart when it is heated
Either class, because both are made of covalently bonded chains
A thermoplastic, because the strong covalent bonds along its chains keep it rigid when hot

questions.prompt: A seal in a cold store must stay rubbery down to -40 C. Which polymer suits it, judging by the glass transition temperature Tg alone?
hints: A polymer is rubbery only above its glass transition temperature. At the lowest working temperature, is each Tg below it or above it?
Compare each Tg with -40 C, remembering that -70 C is colder than -40 C.

acceptedIdeas: The rubber of a rubber band, whose Tg is about -70 C
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The rubber of a rubber band, whose Tg is about -70 C

questions.onCorrect: Tg is about -70 C, which is 30 degrees below the lowest working temperature, so the chains can still move at -40 C and the seal stays soft. Cooled below -70 C the rubber would turn glassy and could snap like a stick of glass.

misconceptions.feedback: Below its Tg of about 100 C polystyrene is glassy, so at -40 C, and at room temperature too, it is hard and brittle rather than rubbery.
A Tg of about 80 C puts -40 C far below it, where the chains are frozen in place and the polymer is hard and brittle.
At -40 C this rubber is 20 degrees below its Tg, so it has turned glassy and can crack, although it would feel soft at room temperature.

choices.label: The rubber of a rubber band, whose Tg is about -70 C
PVC, a hard plastic with a Tg of about 80 C
Polystyrene, a glassy plastic with a Tg of about 100 C
A rubber compound whose Tg is about -20 C

questions.prompt: A bar of a ceramic is tested twice, once pulled in tension and once squeezed in compression. How do the failure stresses compare?
hints: Think about what each load does to a small flaw in the surface.
A crack grows when it is pulled open and stays shut when it is squeezed. Decide which loading lets a flaw run.

acceptedIdeas: Compression is much higher than tension.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression is much higher than tension.

questions.onCorrect: Ceramics are often used in compression, such as bricks and concrete, for this reason.

misconceptions.feedback: A flaw in a ceramic opens under tension, so the failure stress is low there. A metal would yield first instead.
The bonds are the same, but a flaw behaves differently: tension opens it and compression closes it.

choices.label: Compression is much higher than tension.
They are about the same, because the bonds are the same.
Tension is much higher than compression.

questions.prompt: For the same composite, with Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3 GPa and 60 percent fibre, what is the stiffness across the fibres, in GPa to two decimal places?
hints: Write 1 / E as the fibre fraction over Ef plus the matrix fraction over Em.
Work out both terms, add them, and take the reciprocal.
The answer is only a little more than twice the matrix stiffness.
questions.onCorrect: Across the fibres the soft matrix dominates, so the composite is only about 2.5 times as stiff as the epoxy, and 19 times less stiff than along the fibres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness along the fibres, where the stiffnesses add by volume. Across them, the compliances add.
That averages the two stiffnesses without weighting them by volume.

questions.prompt: A glass-fibre composite has fibres with Ef = 70 GPa and a matrix with Em = 3 GPa, and 50 percent fibre by volume. What is its stiffness along the fibres, in GPa?
hints: Along the fibres the stiffnesses add in proportion to volume.
Multiply each stiffness by its volume fraction.
Add the two products.
questions.onCorrect: The fibres supply 35 of the 36.5 GPa, since they are far stiffer than the matrix.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness across the fibres. Along them, add the stiffnesses weighted by volume.
That adds the two stiffnesses and leaves out the volume fractions.

questions.prompt: For the same glass-fibre composite, with Ef = 70 GPa, Em = 3 GPa and 50 percent fibre, find the stiffness across the fibres, in GPa to two decimal places.
hints: Across the fibres the compliances, 1 / E, add in proportion to volume.
Take the reciprocal.
questions.onCorrect: Across the fibres the composite is more than six times less stiff than along them, which is why layers of fibre are laid in several directions.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stiffness along the fibres. Across them, add the compliances, 1 / E.
That is 1 / E. Take its reciprocal to get E.

questions.prompt: A carbon-fibre composite with 60 percent fibre (Ef = 230 GPa, Em = 3 GPa) has a stiffness of 139 GPa along its fibres and 7.4 GPa across them. A strip cut from a plate of it is to be pulled along its length, and it must be as stiff as possible in that direction. How should the fibres run?
hints: Along the fibres the fibre and matrix stretch by the same strain, and across them the load passes through both in turn.
Which direction of pull gives the large stiffness of 139 GPa, and which gives the small one of 7.4 GPa?

acceptedIdeas: All along the strip, so that its stiffness is about 139 GPa
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All along the strip, so that its stiffness is about 139 GPa

questions.onCorrect: The strip is pulled along its length, so the fibres have to lie along it, where they carry most of the load at 139 GPa. A part loaded in several directions needs layers of fibre laid in each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: The fibres across the strip add almost nothing to its stiffness along it, because the load reaches them in series with the soft matrix. Half of the fibre does no work, and the stiffness falls to roughly half of 139 GPa.
Across the fibres the soft matrix controls the result, giving only 7.4 GPa, nearly 19 times less than along them.

choices.label: All across the strip, so that the matrix is the part that is reinforced
Half along the strip and half across it, so that it is stiff both ways
All along the strip, so that its stiffness is about 139 GPa

questions.prompt: Each line describes a polymer part. Is the polymer a thermoplastic or a thermoset?
hints: Ask whether heating the part could let its chains slide past each other.
Cross-links tie the chains into one network, and secondary bonds alone leave them free to slide when warmed.
questions.onCorrect: A polymer that can be softened, shaped and set again has free chains and is a thermoplastic, and one that fixes its shape on curing has cross-links and is a thermoset.

items.label: A lid that softens and sags in boiling water, then stiffens again as it cools
items.explanation: Its chains slide when warmed and set again on cooling, which is how a thermoplastic behaves.

items.label: A bottle that is shredded, melted and moulded into new products
items.explanation: Only a polymer whose chains are free to slide when heated can be melted and shaped many times.

items.label: A carrier bag whose chains are held together by weak secondary bonds only
items.explanation: With nothing but secondary bonds between the chains, the polymer softens and flows when warmed.

items.label: A glue joint that stays solid until it chars in a flame
items.explanation: A thermoset cannot melt, because its chains are tied together, and it decomposes if heated enough.

items.label: A resin that cured into one network and cannot be reshaped by heating
items.explanation: Curing joins the chains by covalent cross-links, and the shape is fixed from then on.

items.label: A rubber whose chains are tied to each other by cross-links
items.explanation: Cross-links make the whole piece one network, so its chains cannot slide apart.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lid, the bottle and the carrier bag are thermoplastics, and the glue joint, the cured resin and the cross-linked rubber are thermosets.

questions.prompt: A designer is looking for jobs for ceramic parts. Which job plays against the way that ceramics fail?
hints: A flaw in a ceramic opens when the part is pulled and closes when it is squeezed.
Which of the three jobs puts the part in tension?

acceptedIdeas: A rod that hangs a heavy lamp from a ceiling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A rod that hangs a heavy lamp from a ceiling

questions.onCorrect: A hanging rod is pulled, which opens any surface flaw and lets a crack run at a stress far below what the bonds could carry. The two other jobs squeeze the ceramic, which keeps its flaws shut.

misconceptions.feedback: The block is squeezed, and compression closes the flaws in it instead of opening them. Thick glass blocks serve in compression for that reason.
A brick carries the wall above it in compression, where flaws are squeezed shut. Bricks and concrete are ceramics used this way for good reason.

choices.label: A thick glass block in a wall, carrying the weight of the wall above it
A rod that hangs a heavy lamp from a ceiling
A brick in a house wall

questions.prompt: A steel plate carries a stress of 100 MPa and has a crack 1 mm long. Take Y = 1. What is the stress intensity at the crack tip, in MPa times the square root of metres, to one decimal place?
hints: The stress intensity grows with the stress and with the square root of the crack length.
Convert 1 mm to metres before taking the square root.
Multiply 100 MPa by the square root of pi times 0.001.
questions.onCorrect: At 5.6 this is far below the toughness of steel, about 50, so the crack does not grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses a in millimetres. The formula needs the crack length in metres.
That leaves out the stress of 100 MPa as a multiplier.

questions.prompt: A crack in a steel part grows to twice its length, while the part and the material stay the same. Roughly how does the stress at which the crack will run change?
hints: The stress intensity grows with the square root of the crack length.
Doubling the length multiplies its square root by about 1.41.

acceptedIdeas: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.

questions.onCorrect: Halving the critical stress needs a crack four times as long, because of the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: The toughness of the material is the same, but a longer crack concentrates the stress more, so a lower applied stress is enough to make it run.
Halving would follow if the stress went as 1 over the crack length, but the stress intensity grows with the square root of the length, so the stress falls by 1 / sqrt(2), about 0.71.
A longer crack concentrates more stress at its tip, so it runs at a lower applied stress.

choices.label: It falls, but only to about 0.7 of what it was.
It stays the same, because the material is the same.
It rises, because a longer crack spreads the load.
It falls to about half.

questions.prompt: The worked example turns the crack length of 2 mm into 0.002 m before it is used. Why?
hints: Look at the unit of K_IC: MPa times the square root of what?
A formula gives the right answer only when each quantity is in the unit that its constants were measured in.

acceptedIdeas: K_IC is in MPa times the square root of metres, so the length has to be in metres
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: K_IC is in MPa times the square root of metres, so the length has to be in metres

questions.onCorrect: The units of K_IC, MPa times the square root of metres, need the crack length in metres. With a = 0.002 m the critical stress is 631 MPa.

misconceptions.feedback: Millimetres measure a 2 mm crack well. What matters is the unit of the formula: using 2 in place of 0.002 would make the critical stress about 32 times too small, 20 MPa instead of 631 MPa.

A square root can be taken of a length in any unit. The trouble is that K_IC was measured with the stress in MPa and the length in metres, so a length in millimetres gives an answer in the wrong units and about 32 times too small.

choices.label: K_IC is in MPa times the square root of metres, so the length has to be in metres
Millimetres cannot go under a square root, so the length must be converted first
A crack of 2 mm is too small to be measured in millimetres with any accuracy

questions.prompt: A steel with K_IC = 50 MPa sqrt(m) carries 200 MPa, with Y = 1. What is the critical crack length, in mm to one decimal place?
hints: The crack runs when K reaches K_IC, so set Y x stress x square root of (pi x a) equal to K_IC and solve for a.
Divide 50 by 200 and square the result, then divide by pi to get a in metres.
Multiply by 1000 to get millimetres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (50 / 200)^2 = 0.0625, divided by pi is 0.01989 m, which is 19.9 mm.

questions.onCorrect: At 200 MPa the steel tolerates a crack of nearly 20 mm, where at 400 MPa the limit is about 5 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a in metres. Multiply by 1000 for millimetres.
That leaves out dividing by pi.

questions.prompt: Two broken bars of the same low-carbon steel come from impact tests, one made at 20 C and one at -40 C. This steel has a ductile-brittle transition near 0 C. Bar A has a rough, jagged fracture surface with shear lips at its edges, and it has narrowed across the break. Bar B has a flat fracture surface with small flat facets, and it snapped in two with no narrowing. Which bar was tested at -40 C, and what does the surface show?
hints: A ductile fracture leaves signs of yielding, such as narrowing of the bar. What would a fracture with no yielding look like?
Which bar was loaded below the transition, where the plastic zone disappears and a crack runs with little energy?

acceptedIdeas: Bar B, which broke below the transition with little yielding, so it absorbed little energy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bar B, which broke below the transition with little yielding, so it absorbed little energy

questions.onCorrect: Bar B has the flat facets and no narrowing of a crack that ran with no yielding, as this steel breaks below its transition. Bar A shows narrowing and shear lips, so it was the 20 C test and absorbed far more energy.

misconceptions.feedback: A rough, jagged surface with shear lips and narrowing is the mark of yielding, which absorbs a great deal of energy. It is how the steel breaks above its transition.
A flat surface with small facets shows a crack that ran across the section with no plastic zone to blunt it, which takes little energy. The ductile bar is the rough one.
The same steel can break either way. Below its transition the plastic zone disappears, and the fracture surface records which way each bar broke.

choices.label: Bar A, because a rough surface shows that the steel was brittle
Neither can be told, because both bars are the same steel
Bar B, because a flat surface shows that it absorbed more energy before it broke
Bar B, which broke below the transition with little yielding, so it absorbed little energy

questions.prompt: A high-strength steel has K_IC = 30 MPa sqrt(m) and works at 600 MPa. What is its critical crack length, in mm to one decimal place?
hints: Divide 30 by 600 and square it.
Divide by pi to get metres.
Convert to millimetres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (30 / 600)^2 = 0.0025, divided by pi is 0.000796 m, which is 0.8 mm.

questions.onCorrect: The stronger steel tolerates a crack of 0.8 mm, against 5.0 mm for a tougher one at 400 MPa, so strength alone does not make a part safer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a in metres. Multiply by 1000 for millimetres.
That leaves out dividing by pi.

questions.prompt: A steel has K_IC = 60 MPa sqrt(m), Y = 1 and a crack of length 1 mm. What stress makes the crack grow, in MPa to the nearest 10?
hints: Convert 1 mm to metres, 0.001 m.
Compute the square root of pi x 0.001.
Divide 60 by it.
questions.onCorrect: Even a 1 mm crack lets the steel carry more than 1000 MPa, but the margin falls quickly as the crack grows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the square root of pi times a. The critical stress divides K_IC by it.
That uses a in millimetres. The formula needs metres.

questions.prompt:
A plate is loaded to 200 MPa, with Y = 1. Inspectors can reliably find cracks 5 mm long or longer, and a crack has to be found before it reaches its critical length. K_IC is in MPa times the square root of metres. Which materials can be used on that basis?

`Soda-lime glass     0.7`
`Alumina              4`
`Aluminium alloy     30`
`Steel               50`
hints: For each material, find the critical crack length at 200 MPa from its K_IC.
A material is usable when its critical length is longer than the 5 mm that inspectors can find.
Remember to turn metres into millimetres before comparing with 5 mm.

acceptedIdeas: The aluminium alloy and the steel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The aluminium alloy and the steel

questions.onCorrect: The critical lengths at 200 MPa are 0.004 mm for the glass, 0.13 mm for alumina, 7.2 mm for the alloy and 19.9 mm for the steel. Only the last two exceed 5 mm, so a crack in them can be found before it runs.

misconceptions.feedback: At 200 MPa the aluminium alloy tolerates a crack of (30 / 200)^2 / pi = 7.2 mm. That is longer than the 5 mm that inspectors can find, so a crack in it is found before it runs.
Alumina tolerates a crack of only 0.13 mm at 200 MPa, far shorter than the 5 mm that inspectors can find, so a crack in it could run before anyone saw it.
Every material has a critical crack length, and what decides is how it compares with the shortest crack that inspectors find. The alloy's 7.2 mm and the steel's 19.9 mm are both above 5 mm.

choices.label: None of them, because every material fails at some crack length
Every material except the soda-lime glass
The aluminium alloy and the steel
The steel only

questions.prompt: A welded structure in a low-carbon steel with a ductile-brittle transition is to work in cold sea water. Which change makes a crack in it more dangerous?
hints: Think about the steel's energy absorbed against temperature.
A crack is more dangerous when the steel absorbs less energy as it fractures. Check which options move the steel towards that low end, and which do not touch its toughness at all.

acceptedIdeas: A lower temperature of the sea water.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A lower temperature of the sea water.

questions.onCorrect: Brittle fractures in welded ships in cold seas in the 1940s were of this kind.

misconceptions.feedback: Paint protects the surface from corrosion but does not change how the steel fractures.
A higher yield strength with the same K_IC changes the stress at which the steel yields, but not the stress at which a crack runs.
A lower load reduces the stress at the crack tip, so it makes a crack safer.

choices.label: A lower load on the structure.
A higher yield strength with the same toughness.
A lower temperature of the sea water.
A thicker coat of paint.

questions.prompt: A drop of salt water sits on a steel plate. Electrons are measured flowing through the steel from the middle of the drop towards its edge, where oxygen takes them up. Where is the steel being lost?
hints: Iron dissolves when its atoms give up electrons. Which end of the electron path is that?
Electrons travel from the site that releases them to the site that uses them up.

acceptedIdeas: In the middle of the drop, where the iron gives up its electrons
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the middle of the drop, where the iron gives up its electrons

questions.onCorrect: The electrons start at iron atoms that dissolve as Fe2+, so metal is lost where they start. Oxygen uses them up at the edge, which loses no metal, so a pit can form under a drop while the steel around it looks sound.

misconceptions.feedback: At the edge the electrons are used up by oxygen, and the metal there does not dissolve. Metal is lost where electrons are released, at the other end of their path.
Metal is lost only where iron atoms give up electrons and dissolve. The place where the electrons are used up loses no metal.
The electrons come from iron atoms as they dissolve as Fe2+ ions. The steel is only the path the electrons take, and the iron that released them goes into the water.

choices.label: In the middle of the drop, where the iron gives up its electrons
Equally at both places, since the current passes through both
At the edge of the drop, where oxygen takes up electrons
Nowhere, because the electrons stay inside the steel

questions.prompt: Aluminium gives up electrons more readily than iron does. Aluminium rivets hold together two large steel plates, and the joint is sprayed with salt water. Which metal corrodes first?
hints: Metal is lost at the anode of the cell, where atoms give up electrons.
Ask which of the two metals gives up electrons more readily.

acceptedIdeas: The aluminium rivets.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The aluminium rivets.

questions.onCorrect: The aluminium is the anode and the large steel plates are the cathode, which makes the small rivets lose metal quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: In a joint the more active metal is the anode. Aluminium is more active than iron, so it is the aluminium that is lost.
Joining different metals in an electrolyte makes a galvanic cell, which makes corrosion faster for the more active metal.

choices.label: The aluminium rivets.
The steel plates, because iron rusts.
Neither, because the metals are different.

questions.prompt: In the worked example each iron atom gives up two electrons as it dissolves as Fe2+, and n = 2 goes under the line in the formula for the mass lost. Why does n divide the mass?
hints: Each atom of iron that dissolves needs the current to carry away two electrons.
If every atom takes more electrons, how many atoms can the same charge dissolve?

acceptedIdeas: Each atom takes n electrons, so a given charge dissolves 1 / n as many atoms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each atom takes n electrons, so a given charge dissolves 1 / n as many atoms

questions.onCorrect: A charge of 315,600 C carries 3.27 mol of electrons, and each iron atom takes two of them, so 1.64 mol of iron dissolves. That is why the moles of metal are the moles of electrons divided by n.

misconceptions.feedback: The weight of each atom is already in the molar mass M. The number n counts the electrons that each atom gives up, and it says nothing about how heavy the ion is.
The charge in coulombs is the current times the time, I x t. The constant F turns moles of electrons into coulombs, and n says how many electrons each atom needs.

choices.label: A larger n means a heavier ion, so less of the metal dissolves for the same current
The number n converts the current in amperes into a charge in coulombs for the formula
Each atom takes n electrons, so a given charge dissolves 1 / n as many atoms

questions.prompt: A zinc sacrificial anode (M = 65.38 g/mol) dissolves as Zn2+ and supplies a current of 0.02 A for one year, 3.156 x 10^7 s. How many grams of zinc are lost?
hints: The charge that flows is the current times the time.
Each zinc atom that dissolves gives up as many electrons as the charge on its ion, written beside Zn.
Divide the charge by n x F for the moles of zinc, then multiply by the molar mass.
questions.onCorrect: A 2 kg zinc anode with this current would last about nine years.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out dividing by n = 2.

questions.prompt: Standard electrode potentials are Mg -2.37 V, Al -1.66 V, Zn -0.76 V, Fe -0.44 V and Cu +0.34 V. Each of these metals is joined to a partner in a wet joint. Does it lose metal, or is it protected?
hints: In each pair, compare the two potentials. Which metal is the more negative?
The more negative metal is the more active one, and the other metal of the pair is the cathode.
questions.onCorrect: In every couple the metal with the more negative potential gives up the electrons and dissolves, and the metal it is joined to is protected for as long as it lasts.

items.label: Zinc, bolted to a steel hull
items.explanation: Zinc has the more negative potential, -0.76 V against -0.44 V, so it is the anode and dissolves in place of the steel.

items.label: The steel hull, with a zinc block bolted to it
items.explanation: The steel is the cathode of the cell, so it loses no metal while the zinc lasts.

items.label: Aluminium rivets in a steel plate
items.explanation: Aluminium, at -1.66 V, is more active than iron, so it is the anode, and a small anode against a large cathode corrodes fast.

items.label: The steel plate that the aluminium rivets hold
items.explanation: The steel is the cathode of the cell, and the rivets pay for that.

items.label: Iron nails holding copper sheeting
items.explanation: Iron, at -0.44 V, is more active than copper at +0.34 V, so the nails are the anode and dissolve.

items.label: The copper sheeting held by iron nails
items.explanation: Copper is the nobler metal and the cathode of the cell, so it loses no metal.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The zinc, the aluminium rivets and the iron nails lose metal, and the steel hull, the steel plate and the copper sheeting are protected.

questions.prompt: A steel part corrodes at a steady 0.01 A. How long will it take to lose 10 g of iron (M = 55.85 g/mol, n = 2), in days to the nearest day?
hints: Rearrange m = I x t x M / (n x F) to make t the subject.
t = m x n x F / (I x M), in seconds.
Divide the seconds by 86,400 to get days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: t = m x n x F / (I x M) = 10 x 2 x 96485 / (0.01 x 55.85) = 3.455e6 s, which is 40 days.

questions.onCorrect: A corrosion current of only 10 mA removes 10 g of iron in about six weeks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. Divide by 86,400 for days.
That divides in the wrong order. The mass is on the top of the fraction.

questions.prompt: A boat's steel hull is protected by a 2.0 kg zinc anode (M = 65.38 g/mol, dissolving as Zn2+) that supplies an average current of 0.05 A. Assuming that all of the zinc dissolves, how many years does the anode last before it has to be replaced, to one decimal place? Take a year as 3.156 x 10^7 s.
hints: Find how many moles of zinc there are in 2.0 kg, then how many moles of electrons they release.
Each mole of electrons carries 96,485 C, and the time follows from the charge divided by the current.
Convert the seconds into years with 3.156 x 10^7 s in a year.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2000 g / 65.38 g/mol = 30.6 mol of zinc, which releases 61.2 mol of electrons. That is 61.2 x 96,485 = 5.90 x 10^6 C, and at 0.05 A it takes 1.18 x 10^8 s, which is 3.7 years.

questions.onCorrect: A current of only 0.05 A uses up 2 kg of zinc in under four years, which is why sacrificial anodes are inspected and replaced on a schedule.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the factor of n = 2. Each zinc atom gives up two electrons, so dissolving the zinc takes twice the charge that this figure uses, and the anode lasts twice as long.
That is the time in seconds. Divide by 3.156 x 10^7 to get years.

questions.prompt: A copper pipe is joined to a steel pipe in wet conditions. Which metal corrodes?
hints: Compare the electrode potentials of iron and copper.
The more active metal of a joined pair is the one that loses metal. Decide which of iron and copper is the more active before you read the options.

acceptedIdeas: The steel, because it is more active than copper.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steel, because it is more active than copper.

questions.onCorrect: The steel is the anode of the galvanic cell, and copper is the cathode, which loses no metal.

misconceptions.feedback: Value has nothing to do with it. The more active metal is the anode, and copper is the less active of the two.
Copper is noble, but the contact makes the steel the anode of a cell, so the steel corrodes faster.
One metal is the anode and the other the cathode, so only the anode loses metal.

choices.label: The steel, because it is more active than copper.
Neither, because copper is noble and protects the steel.
Both corrode at the same rate.
The copper, because copper is the more valuable metal.

questions.prompt: Steel roofing sheet will be scratched by ladders and tools in a wet climate, and each scratch will expose bare steel. Which finish keeps the steel from rusting at a scratch?
hints: At a scratch, steel and the coating are both in contact with the wet air. Which of the two is the more active metal?
A coating protects a scratch only if it makes the exposed steel the cathode.

acceptedIdeas: Zinc, which stays the anode and corrodes in place of the exposed steel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zinc, which stays the anode and corrodes in place of the exposed steel

questions.onCorrect: Zinc is more active than iron, so even where the coating is scratched the zinc is the anode and the exposed steel is the cathode, which stays protected until the zinc is used up.

misconceptions.feedback: Paint is only a barrier. At a scratch the bare steel is exposed, and the rust can spread underneath the paint around it.
Copper is the less active metal, +0.34 V against -0.44 V for iron. At a scratch the steel becomes the anode, and a large copper area draws its current from a small patch of steel.

choices.label: Zinc, which stays the anode and corrodes in place of the exposed steel
Paint, because it keeps water off the whole surface of the sheet
Copper plating, because copper is a metal that corrodes only very slowly

questions.prompt:
Four test pieces are cast from the same metal in the same sand. Which one freezes last?

`Plate   400 x 300 x 20 mm`
`Block   100 x 100 x 50 mm`
`Cube    60 mm on a side`
`Rod     20 mm across and 200 mm long`
hints: Heat leaves through the surface, so compare the metal behind each square millimetre of surface for the four pieces.
Work out V / A for each piece from its volume and its whole surface area.

acceptedIdeas: The block, which has the most metal behind each square millimetre of surface
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The block, which has the most metal behind each square millimetre of surface

questions.onCorrect: V / A is 8.96 mm for the plate, 12.5 mm for the block, 10.0 mm for the cube and 4.76 mm for the rod. Time goes as the square of the ratio, so the block takes about 1.6 times as long as the cube.

misconceptions.feedback: The plate holds the most metal, 2,400 cm3, but it also has a large surface. Its V / A is 9.0 mm against 12.5 mm for the block, and the freezing time goes with V / A, not with the volume.
Equal sides do not decide it. For a cube V / A is the side divided by 6, which is 10.0 mm here and is less than the block's 12.5 mm.
The length of a piece does not decide it. A thin rod has a large surface for its volume, so its V / A is only 4.8 mm, and it freezes first.

choices.label: The plate, because it is the piece that holds the most metal of the four
The block, which has the most metal behind each square millimetre of surface
The rod, because its length gives it the greatest distance for heat to travel
The cube, because every one of its sides is equal in length to the others

questions.prompt: A cube of side 200 mm is cast in the same mould material as a cube of side 100 mm, so its ratio of volume to surface area, V / A, is twice as large. Roughly how much longer does the larger cube take to freeze?
hints: Heat leaves through the surface, so compare how much metal lies behind each square millimetre of surface.
The larger cube has eight times the volume and four times the surface area.

acceptedIdeas: About four times as long.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About four times as long.

questions.onCorrect: Freezing time goes with the square of V / A, so doubling the ratio gives four times the time, even though the larger cube holds eight times the metal.

misconceptions.feedback: The mould is the same, but the larger cube has twice as much metal behind each square millimetre of surface, so it takes longer to lose its heat.
The time grows faster than V / A, because Chvorinov's rule makes it depend on the square of V / A, so twice the ratio gives four times the time.
The larger cube holds eight times the metal, but it also has four times the surface to lose heat through, so its freezing time grows by less than eight.

choices.label: About the same time, because the mould is the same.
About four times as long.
About eight times as long, in step with the volume.
About twice as long, in step with V / A.

questions.prompt: The worked example finds the freezing time from V / A and not from the volume alone. Why?
hints: Where does the heat of a freezing casting leave it?
A flat plate and a compact block of equal volume have different surfaces. Which of the two would freeze sooner?

acceptedIdeas: Heat leaves through the surface, so the metal behind each unit of surface sets the time
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heat leaves through the surface, so the metal behind each unit of surface sets the time

questions.onCorrect: The metal gives its heat to the mould through the surface, so a casting with a lot of metal behind each square millimetre of surface takes longest. Chvorinov's rule squares that ratio to get the time.

misconceptions.feedback: The volume is easy to find. Volume alone does not decide the time, because two pieces of equal volume freeze at different times when their surfaces differ.
A thin plate and a thick block can have the same surface area and freeze at very different times. The ratio of volume to surface, the metal behind each unit of surface, sets the time.

choices.label: The volume of a casting cannot be measured accurately once the metal is inside the mould
Heat leaves through the surface, so the metal behind each unit of surface sets the time
Only the surface area matters, whatever amount of metal lies behind that surface

questions.prompt: Now cast a cube of side 50 mm, with the same B = 2 min/cm2. What is the freezing time, in minutes to two decimal places?
hints: For a cube, V / A is the side divided by 6, and the side is 5 cm.
Square V / A, then multiply by B = 2.
The time is about a quarter of the 5.56 minutes of the larger cube.
questions.onCorrect: The small cube freezes in 1.39 minutes, a quarter of the 5.56 minutes for the cube of 100 mm.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies V / A by 2 without squaring it first.
That leaves out the mould constant B = 2.

questions.prompt: A casting is to be 490 mm long after it has cooled, and the metal shrinks 2 percent in length as it cools. How long, in mm, must the pattern be?
hints: The casting is 98 percent of the pattern.
Divide the casting length by 0.98.
Do not add 2 percent to 490.
questions.onCorrect: The pattern is 500 mm, and 2 percent of 500 mm is 10 mm, which is the shrinkage in the casting.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 percent of 490 to the casting length. The 2 percent is of the pattern, not the casting.
That subtracts the allowance. The pattern must be larger than the casting.

questions.prompt: One large casting is needed, once, for a prototype that will be machined afterwards. Which casting process fits best?
hints: The tooling cost must stay low for a single part.
Compare what each process costs to set up and what it costs per part, then ask which of those matters when you need only one part.

acceptedIdeas: Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.

questions.onCorrect: Sand casting uses a cheap, expendable mould, so the cost per part is high but the cost of starting is low.

misconceptions.feedback: Die casting needs a steel mould that costs a great deal, and that pays back only over thousands of parts.
For a single part the tooling is the whole difference, since a die costs a great deal and a sand pattern very little.

choices.label: Die casting, because its parts come out accurate and cheap.
Either, because for a single part the tooling cost makes no difference.
Sand casting, because its pattern is cheap.

questions.prompt: A casting section has V / A = 1.2 cm. The foundry adds a riser with V / A = 1.0 cm, and the mould constant B is the same for both. After the casting is cut up, a shrinkage cavity is found in the section next to the riser. What happened?
hints: Compare the freezing times of the riser and the section with t = B x (V / A)^2.
A riser can feed the casting only while it is still liquid. Which of the two freezes first here?

acceptedIdeas: The riser froze first, in 0.69 of the section's time, so it had no liquid left to feed it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The riser froze first, in 0.69 of the section's time, so it had no liquid left to feed it

questions.onCorrect: The riser's time is (1.0 / 1.2)^2 = 0.69 of the section's, so it solidified long before the section had finished contracting. The riser needs a larger V / A than the section, so that it freezes last and takes the cavity with it.

misconceptions.feedback: A riser that froze last would hold the cavity itself. Here the riser's V / A of 1.0 cm is smaller than the section's 1.2 cm, so the riser freezes first.
The shrinkage allowance on the pattern sets the final size of the casting. A cavity inside the metal shows a section that froze with no liquid left to feed it, which the pattern does not affect.

choices.label: The pattern was too small, so the casting shrank below its size and left a cavity inside
The riser froze after the section, so the cavity formed in the riser, as it was meant to do
The riser froze first, in 0.69 of the section's time, so it had no liquid left to feed it

questions.prompt: A cast bracket has a thin web, with V / A of about 5 mm, and a thick boss, with V / A of about 20 mm. A shrinkage cavity turns up inside the boss and not in the web. Why there, and what is the usual remedy?
hints: Compare the freezing times of web and boss, using the fact that time goes as the square of V / A.
A shrinkage cavity forms in the last place to freeze. Which part of the bracket is that?

acceptedIdeas: The boss froze last, with nothing left to feed it, so add a riser over it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The boss froze last, with nothing left to feed it, so add a riser over it

questions.onCorrect: The freezing times are in the ratio (20 / 5)^2 = 16, so the web is solid long before the boss. The boss then shrinks with no liquid supply, and a riser placed over it, or a thinner boss, removes the cavity.

misconceptions.feedback: The thin web has the smaller V / A, so it freezes first, in about one sixteenth of the boss's time. It is the boss, the last part to freeze, that has no liquid left to feed its shrinkage.
A shrinkage cavity records metal that froze with no liquid left to feed its contraction, and it forms in the thickest part, the last to freeze. Venting would not feed it.

choices.label: The boss froze last, with nothing left to feed it, so add a riser over it
The web froze last and drew liquid out of the boss, so the web should be made thicker
Gas was trapped in the boss, so the mould needs a vent above the boss to let it out

questions.prompt: A casting is made in a sand mould with a riser. In what order do these things happen?
hints: The pattern has to come out before any metal can fill the space that it leaves.
The shrinkage hole forms in the last metal to freeze, which the riser is designed to be.
questions.onCorrect: The riser can feed the casting only while it is liquid, so it has to freeze after the casting, and the hole it collects is then cut away with it.

items: Sand is packed round the pattern, which is then removed to leave the cavity
Liquid metal is poured into the cavity and the riser
The casting freezes while the riser is still liquid and feeds it
The riser freezes last, with the shrinkage hole in it

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mould is made round the pattern, metal is poured in, the casting freezes while the liquid riser feeds it, and the riser freezes last and takes the shrinkage hole with it.

questions.prompt: Why must a riser be shaped so that it freezes after the casting it feeds?
hints: Think about where the shrinkage cavity ends up.
Ask what the casting needs from the riser while the casting is shrinking.

acceptedIdeas: So that it can feed liquid metal to the casting as it shrinks.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: So that it can feed liquid metal to the casting as it shrinks.

questions.onCorrect: A riser that freezes last takes the shrinkage hole into itself, and the sound casting is separated from it afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: A riser that is too small freezes first and cannot feed the casting. It has to be bigger in V / A than the section it feeds.
If both froze together, the casting would have no liquid metal to make up its shrinkage.
Cutting it off is a later step, and it has no effect on whether the casting is sound.

choices.label: So that the casting and the riser freeze at the same time, shrinking evenly.
So that the riser is as small as possible and wastes little metal.
So that it can feed liquid metal to the casting as it shrinks.
So that the riser can be cut off more easily afterwards.

questions.prompt: A billet 50 mm tall with a cross-section of 2000 mm2 is forged down to 20 mm tall. Assuming the volume stays the same, what is the new cross-sectional area, in mm2?
hints: Work out the volume first: height times area.
The volume does not change during forging.
Divide the volume by the new height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The volume is 50 x 2000 = 100,000 mm3, so the new area is 100,000 / 20 = 5000 mm2.

questions.onCorrect: Squeezing metal does not compress it. It makes the billet wider, so the area grows as the height falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales by height ratio the wrong way round. The shorter billet must be wider, not narrower. Divide the volume by 20 mm.
That keeps the area unchanged. The volume is constant, so a shorter billet has a larger area.

questions.prompt: A plate is rolled 25 percent thinner, and then rolled another 25 percent thinner than it is at that point. Roughly what is the total reduction in thickness?
hints: The second 25 percent is a fraction of the thickness after the first pass.
Is 25 percent of a thinner plate more or less than 25 percent of the original?

acceptedIdeas: A little less than 50 percent.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A little less than 50 percent.

questions.onCorrect: The total is 43.75 percent, since 0.75 x 0.75 = 0.5625 of the thickness remains, and percentages of different thicknesses do not add.

misconceptions.feedback: The second 25 percent is taken from a plate that is already thinner, so it removes less than the first did and the total falls short of 50 percent.
Work hardening changes the force needed, but the rolls set the reduction, and the second 25 percent comes off a thinner plate, so the total is below 50 percent.

choices.label: A little more than 50 percent, because the second pass works on harder metal.
Exactly 50 percent, because 25 and 25 make 50.
A little less than 50 percent.

questions.prompt: The second pass takes the plate from 25 mm to 18 mm. What is its true strain, to three decimal places?
hints: True strain is the natural logarithm of the starting thickness over the final thickness.
Divide 25 by 18 first.
ln(1.389) is a little under 0.33.
questions.onCorrect: The two true strains, 0.182 and 0.329, sum to 0.511, which is ln(30 / 18), the strain of rolling 30 mm to 18 mm in one pass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log base 10 of 1.389. True strain uses the natural logarithm.
That is the percent reduction as a fraction. True strain is a logarithm.

questions.prompt: A press can deliver 800 kN. A steel billet 50 mm tall, with a cross-section of 2,000 mm2, has a flow stress of 250 MPa. It is to be squeezed between flat dies down to 25 mm tall. Will the press manage it?
hints: Work out the area of the billet at the end of the stroke from the fact that its volume does not change.
The force on the dies is the flow stress times the area in contact with them. When is that area largest?

acceptedIdeas: No. The area doubles to 4,000 mm2, so the force at the end of the stroke is 1,000 kN
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. The area doubles to 4,000 mm2, so the force at the end of the stroke is 1,000 kN

questions.onCorrect: The volume of 100,000 mm3 stays constant, so at 25 mm tall the area is 4,000 mm2 and the force is 250 x 4,000 = 1,000,000 N, or 1,000 kN. The 800 kN press would stall before the end of the stroke.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force at the start of the stroke. The volume stays constant, so as the billet flattens its area grows to 4,000 mm2, and the force, the flow stress times that area, reaches 1,000 kN.
The shorter billet is wider, and the force is the flow stress times the area in contact with the dies, so the force rises as the billet flattens. A press must be chosen for the end of the stroke.

choices.label: Yes. The force is 250 MPa x 2,000 mm2 = 500 kN, which is below 800 kN
No. The area doubles to 4,000 mm2, so the force at the end of the stroke is 1,000 kN
Yes. The billet gets shorter, so less force is needed as the stroke goes on

questions.prompt: Hot working is done above about half the melting point on the kelvin scale, and cold working below it. Melting points are aluminium 660 C, iron 1,538 C, copper 1,085 C and tungsten 3,422 C. Which of these jobs is hot working, and which is cold working?
hints: Add 273 to each temperature in C to get kelvin, and compare the result with half the melting point in kelvin.
A temperature that is high for one metal can be low for another with a much higher melting point.
questions.onCorrect: Whether working is hot or cold depends on the temperature relative to the metal's own melting point, so a red-hot bar can still be cold worked.

items.label: Iron rolled at 1,100 C
items.explanation: 1,373 K is 0.76 of iron's melting point of 1,811 K, well above half.

items.label: Aluminium rolled at 450 C
items.explanation: 723 K is 0.77 of aluminium's melting point of 933 K, well above half.

items.label: Copper forged at 800 C
items.explanation: 1,073 K is 0.79 of copper's melting point of 1,358 K, well above half.

items.label: Copper wire drawn at 20 C
items.explanation: 293 K is only 0.22 of copper's melting point, far below half, so the wire work hardens.

items.label: An iron bar bent at 400 C
items.explanation: 673 K is 0.37 of iron's melting point, below half, so the iron hardens as it is bent even though it is hot.

items.label: Tungsten worked at 1,000 C
items.explanation: 1,273 K is only 0.34 of tungsten's melting point of 3,695 K, so it is cold working despite the glow.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The iron at 1,100 C, the aluminium at 450 C and the copper at 800 C are hot working, and the copper wire at 20 C, the iron bar at 400 C and the tungsten at 1,000 C are cold working.

questions.prompt: A press-brake operator sets up a 90 degree bend in mild steel sheet, with a yield strength of 250 MPa, and gets it right. The same setting on a high-strength steel sheet of the same thickness, with a yield strength of 900 MPa and the same E of 210 GPa, leaves the part opened out by several degrees. Why, and what should the operator do?
hints: Part of the strain in a bend is elastic and comes back when the load is removed. Which sheet can store more elastic strain?
The elastic strain at yield is the yield strength divided by E. Work it out for both sheets.

acceptedIdeas: The stronger sheet recovers more elastic strain, so bend a little past 90 degrees
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stronger sheet recovers more elastic strain, so bend a little past 90 degrees

questions.onCorrect: Yield strength divided by E gives 0.12 percent for the mild steel and 0.43 percent for the stronger sheet. More of the stronger sheet's strain is elastic, so more of it springs back, and it has to be bent a little past the target.
