misconceptions.feedback: The same tool and setting gave a good bend in the mild steel, so the difference lies in the sheet. The stronger sheet stores more elastic strain, and that part recovers when the tool lifts.
Both sheets have the same E, so neither is stiffer. They differ in yield strength, which sets how much elastic strain a bend can store, and the force does not change the recovery.

choices.label: The high-strength sheet is stiffer, so it resists the bend, and more force is needed
The tool has worn since the first job, so the setting has changed and must be reset
The stronger sheet recovers more elastic strain, so bend a little past 90 degrees

questions.prompt: A sheet 1.5 mm thick is bent through 90 degrees with an inner radius R = 2 mm and K = 0.4. What bend allowance does the bend use up, in mm to two decimal places?
hints: Work out K x t = 0.4 x 1.5.
Add R to find the radius of the neutral axis.
Multiply by pi / 2, which is 1.571.
questions.onCorrect: The flat blank must include 4.08 mm of material for the bend, in addition to the lengths of the two flanges.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the inner radius of 2 mm and leaves out K x t. The neutral axis lies inside the sheet, at R + K x t.
That is the radius of the neutral axis. Multiply it by the angle in radians, pi / 2.

questions.prompt: A sheet 3 mm thick is bent through 60 degrees, with R = 5 mm and K = 0.33. What is the bend allowance, in mm to two decimal places?
hints: Work out K x t = 0.33 x 3.
The angle in radians is pi / 3 = 1.047.
Multiply the radius of the neutral axis by the angle.
questions.onCorrect: A smaller angle gives a shorter arc, so a 60 degree bend takes less flat length than a 90 degree bend of the same radius.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 90 degrees. The angle here is 60 degrees, which is pi / 3 radians.
That is the radius of the neutral axis. Multiply it by the angle in radians.

questions.prompt: A cold rolling schedule takes a plate from 20 mm to 16 mm in one pass and from 16 mm to 12.8 mm in the next. What is the total true strain of the schedule, to three decimal places?
hints: True strains add from pass to pass, and each is the natural logarithm of the thickness before the pass over the thickness after it.
Work out ln(20 / 16) and ln(16 / 12.8), or the single ln of the first and last thicknesses.
Add the two true strains.
questions.onCorrect: True strains add, so the schedule has a true strain of 0.446. The two reductions of 20 percent look as if they add to 40 percent, but the real reduction is 36 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two engineering reductions, 0.2 and 0.2. Each is measured against a different thickness, so they cannot be added, and true strains can.
That is the true strain of one pass, ln(20 / 16). The schedule has two passes, and their true strains add.

questions.prompt: A bracket has two straight legs, 30 mm and 40 mm long, joined by a 90 degree bend in sheet 1.5 mm thick, with an inner radius of 2 mm and K = 0.4. What length of flat blank does it need?
hints: The blank is the two straight legs plus the length of flat sheet that the bend uses up.
The bend allowance is the arc of the neutral axis, at a radius R + K x t, through an angle in radians.
questions.onCorrect: The bend allowance is (pi / 2) x (2 + 0.4 x 1.5) = 4.08 mm, and the blank is 30 + 40 + 4.08 = 74.08 mm long.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two legs and leaves out the bend. The blank also has to supply the bend allowance, 4.08 mm, for the curved part.
That finds the bend allowance from the inner radius alone, (pi / 2) x 2 = 3.14 mm. The neutral axis lies inside the sheet at R + K x t, which is 2.6 mm from the centre.
That puts the neutral axis at R + t, the outer radius, as if K were 1. With K = 0.4 the radius is 2.6 mm and the allowance is 4.08 mm.

questions.prompt: Job 1 makes 100,000 small steel bolts that need a smooth surface, close dimensions and extra strength. Job 2 forms a large steel billet into a crankshaft shape in a few strokes, using the smallest press that will do it. Which working suits each job?
hints: List what each job needs: surface, tolerance, strength, size of the change of shape, and the size of the press.
One kind of working gives a good surface and strength. The other takes much less force for a large change of shape.

acceptedIdeas: Job 1 by cold working and job 2 by hot working
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Job 1 by cold working and job 2 by hot working

questions.onCorrect: Cold working suits the bolts, since it gives a good surface, close tolerances and a stronger part. Hot working suits the crankshaft, since the flow stress is low and a large change of shape takes a smaller press.

misconceptions.feedback: Hot working leaves an oxidised surface and loose dimensions, which does not suit the bolts. It suits job 2, but job 1 needs the surface, tolerance and strength of cold working.
This is the wrong way round. Cold working gives the bolts their surface, tolerance and extra strength, and for the crankshaft it would need far more force and could crack the metal.
Cold working suits the bolts, but a large change of shape in a few strokes needs the much lower flow stress of hot metal, and a cold billet would need a far bigger press.

choices.label: Both by cold working, because cold working gives the best surface
Job 1 by cold working and job 2 by hot working
Both by hot working, because hot metal is easier to shape
Job 1 by hot working and job 2 by cold working

questions.prompt: A bar of diameter 30 mm is turned at 1,200 rev/min. What is the cutting speed, in m/min to one decimal place?
hints: The surface travels pi x D each revolution.
Multiply pi x 30 mm by 1200 revolutions each minute.
Divide by 1000 to convert mm to m.
questions.onCorrect: The cutting speed is the surface speed past the tool, and it sets how hot the cutting edge gets.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed in mm/min. Divide by 1000 for m/min.
That multiplies D by N and divides by 1000 without the factor of pi.

questions.prompt: In the worked example the removal rate of 112,500 mm3 per minute is turned into mm3 per second before it is multiplied by the specific energy. Why?
hints: Check the units: joules per mm3 times mm3 per second gives what?
A watt is a joule per second.

acceptedIdeas: Power is energy per second, so the removal rate has to be per second to give watts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is energy per second, so the removal rate has to be per second to give watts

questions.onCorrect: The specific energy of 3 J/mm3 times 1,875 mm3/s gives 5,625 J/s, which is 5,625 W. A removal rate per minute would give joules per minute, which is 60 times too large for a power in watts.

misconceptions.feedback: A rate per second is the smaller number: 112,500 per minute becomes 1,875 per second. The conversion is there to make the units give watts, and it does not enlarge the result.
The specific energy is joules per mm3, a quantity with no time in it. Time comes in through power, which is joules per second, and that is why the removal rate has to be per second.

choices.label: Power is energy per second, so the removal rate has to be per second to give watts
The specific energy was measured over one second, so the rate has to match that time
A rate per second is the larger number, so converting makes the power larger

questions.prompt: A cut at 60 m/min with f = 0.1 mm/rev and d = 1 mm removes 6000 mm3/min, which is 100 mm3/s. With a specific cutting energy of 2.5 J/mm3, what power is needed, in W?
hints: Power is specific energy times removal rate.
The units are J/mm3 times mm3/s, which is J/s.
Multiply 2.5 by 100.
questions.onCorrect: Small cuts need little power, so a light machine can take them, but the same energy goes into a smaller chip.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the removal rate per minute. For watts, use mm3 per second.
That is the power in kW. The question asks for watts.

questions.prompt: For a typical carbide tool, tool life varies as the cutting speed raised to the power -4. A cutting speed is raised by 20 percent. What is the likely change in tool life?
hints: A power of -4 divides by the speed ratio four times.
The speed ratio is 1.2, and 1.2 to the power 4 is about 2.07.

acceptedIdeas: It falls by about half.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls by about half.

questions.onCorrect: Taylor's rule gives 1.2 to the power -4, which is 0.48, so the tool lasts about half as long.

misconceptions.feedback: Tool life falls much faster than speed rises, because the wear grows steeply with the temperature at the edge.
Hardness does not protect the edge. The wear rate rises sharply with cutting speed.

choices.label: It falls by about half.
It does not change, because the tool is hard.
It falls by about 17 percent, in proportion to the speed.

questions.prompt: A carbide tool with Taylor exponent n = 0.25 lasts 60 minutes at a cutting speed of 100 m/min. The same kind of tool is then run at 110 m/min. How many minutes does it last, to the nearest minute?
hints: Taylor's equation says that tool life goes as the cutting speed to the power -1 / n.
With n = 0.25 the power is -4. The speed ratio is 1.1, and 1.1 to the power -4 is 1 / 1.4641.
Multiply the 60 minutes by that factor.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The life changes by 1.1^-4 = 0.683, so 60 x 0.683 = 41 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: A rise of 10 percent in speed costs about a third of the tool's life, from 60 minutes to 41.

misconceptions.feedback: That raises 1.1 to the power +4, which lengthens the life. Tool life falls as speed rises, so the exponent is negative.
That divides by 1.1 once, as if the exponent were -1. For n = 0.25 the exponent is -1 / n = -4.

questions.prompt: A carbide tool with Taylor exponent n = 0.25 cuts at a steady speed. The speed is then cut by 20 percent, so each part takes proportionally longer to cut. How many times as many parts does one cutting edge machine before it has to be changed, to two decimal places?
hints: Two things change: the life of the edge, and the time that each part takes.
The life changes by the speed ratio, 0.8, to the power -4. Each part takes 1 / 0.8 times as long.
Divide the factor for life by the factor for time per part.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The life rises by 0.8^-4 = 2.44, and each part takes 1.25 times as long, so one edge cuts 2.44 / 1.25 = 1.95 times as many parts.

questions.onCorrect: Slowing the cut by a fifth nearly doubles the parts cut per edge, which is why the cheapest speed is well below the fastest the tool can stand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the factor for tool life alone. Each part also takes 1.25 times as long to cut, so the number of parts rises by less than the life does.
That multiplies the life factor by the time per part. Parts per edge are the life divided by the time that each part takes.

questions.prompt: A turned surface is cut with a feed of 0.2 mm/rev and a tool nose radius of 0.8 mm. What is the theoretical average roughness Ra, in micrometres to two decimal places?
hints: The theoretical roughness grows with the square of the feed and falls as the nose radius grows.
Divide the square of the feed by 32 times the nose radius, with both in mm.
The result is in mm. Multiply by 1000 for micrometres.
questions.onCorrect: The roughness depends on the feed and the nose radius, and not on the cutting speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Ra in millimetres. Multiply by 1000 for micrometres.
That uses 8 r where the formula has 32 r. Divide f squared by 32 times the nose radius.

questions.prompt: A finishing pass with a tool of nose radius 0.8 mm must give a theoretical Ra of no more than 0.4 micrometres. Which is the coarsest of these feeds that meets the limit?
hints: The theoretical roughness depends on the square of the feed and on the nose radius.
Work out Ra for each feed, and convert the result from mm to micrometres before comparing it with 0.4.

acceptedIdeas: 0.10 mm/rev
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 0.10 mm/rev

questions.onCorrect: At 0.10 mm/rev the roughness is 0.39 micrometres, just inside the limit, and 0.15 mm/rev gives 0.88. Because the feed is squared, halving it quarters the roughness, which is why finishing passes use small feeds.

misconceptions.feedback: That meets the limit, with an Ra of 0.10 micrometres, but a coarser feed meets it too and cuts faster, so this is not the coarsest feed that does.
The roughness is 0.15^2 / (32 x 0.8) = 0.88 micrometres, more than twice the 0.4 allowed.
The roughness is 0.2^2 / (32 x 0.8) = 1.56 micrometres, nearly four times the 0.4 allowed.

choices.label: 0.05 mm/rev
0.10 mm/rev
0.15 mm/rev
0.20 mm/rev

questions.prompt: A carbide tool should cut steel at 120 m/min. What spindle speed, in rev/min to the nearest whole number, does a bar 80 mm in diameter need?
hints: The cutting speed is the distance the surface travels each minute, which is the circumference times the revolutions per minute.
Turn the relation round to find the revolutions per minute from the surface speed, keeping metres and millimetres straight.
Divide 120 x 1000 by the circumference of the bar in mm.
questions.onCorrect: A smaller bar needs a higher spindle speed for the same cutting speed, since its surface travels less far in each turn.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the radius of the bar, 40 mm, in place of its diameter. The surface travels pi x D in each turn, with D the full diameter.
That leaves out the factor of 1000 between metres and millimetres. The diameter is in mm and the speed in m/min.

questions.prompt:
A lathe cuts the same steel in four setups, each with a cutting speed v in m/min, a feed f in mm/rev and a depth d in mm.

`A   v 200   f 0.10   d 1.0`
`B   v 100   f 0.40   d 1.5`
`C   v  60   f 0.25   d 3.0`
`D   v 120   f 0.30   d 2.0`

Which setup needs the most power from the spindle motor?
hints: In a given material the power is proportional to the volume of metal removed each second.
Work out v x f x d for each setup, with the speed in mm/min, and compare.

acceptedIdeas: Setup D, which removes 1,200 mm3 of metal each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Setup D, which removes 1,200 mm3 of metal each second

questions.onCorrect: The removal rates are 333, 1,000, 750 and 1,200 mm3/s. At a specific cutting energy of 3 J/mm3 these need 1.0, 3.0, 2.25 and 3.6 kW, and setup D needs the most.

misconceptions.feedback: Setup A removes only 333 mm3/s, because its feed and depth are small. The power in a given steel follows the removal rate, v x f x d, and not the speed alone.
Setup B removes 1,000 mm3/s, which is less than the 1,200 mm3/s of setup D. The feed is only one of the three settings in the removal rate.
Setup C removes 750 mm3/s. A deep cut at a low speed and a moderate feed gives a smaller removal rate than setup D.

choices.label: Setup B, because it has the highest feed
Setup C, because it has the deepest cut
Setup A, because it has the highest cutting speed
Setup D, which removes 1,200 mm3 of metal each second

questions.prompt: A turned shaft comes off the lathe with fine spiral ridges that a fingernail can feel, and the drawing asks for a smoother finish. The lathe runs at 100 m/min with a feed of 0.3 mm/rev, a depth of cut of 2 mm and a tool nose radius of 0.8 mm. Which single change improves the finish most?
hints: The ridges are left by the tool nose as the work advances by one feed in each revolution.
Which of the four settings appears in the formula for the theoretical roughness, and which way does each one push it?

acceptedIdeas: Halve the feed, from 0.3 to 0.15 mm/rev, which cuts Ra to a quarter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Halve the feed, from 0.3 to 0.15 mm/rev, which cuts Ra to a quarter

questions.onCorrect: The roughness is f^2 / (32 r), so with f = 0.3 and r = 0.8 it is 3.5 micrometres, and halving the feed brings it to 0.88. Speed and depth do not enter it, and a smaller nose radius makes it worse.

misconceptions.feedback: The theoretical roughness depends on the feed and the nose radius, and it has no speed term, so a faster cut leaves the same ridges.
A smaller radius makes the ridges deeper, not shallower. The roughness doubles, from 3.5 to 7.0 micrometres.
The depth of cut does not enter the theoretical roughness, so a deeper cut leaves the ridges as they are and only raises the removal rate.

choices.label: Halve the feed, from 0.3 to 0.15 mm/rev, which cuts Ra to a quarter
Halve the nose radius to 0.4 mm, so that the tool tip is sharper
Double the depth of cut to 4 mm, so that fewer passes are needed
Double the cutting speed to 200 m/min, so the tool passes each ridge faster

questions.prompt: A moulded lid has a footprint of 200 mm by 100 mm, seen along the direction in which the mould opens, and walls 30 mm deep. The cavity pressure is 40 MPa, and the shop's press clamps with 1,000 kN. Can it mould the lid?
hints: The mould halves are pushed apart by the cavity pressure acting over the area that faces the direction of opening.
Which area is that for a box-shaped lid: the footprint, or the footprint plus the walls?

acceptedIdeas: Yes. The projected area is 20,000 mm2, so the clamp force needed is 800 kN
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes. The projected area is 20,000 mm2, so the clamp force needed is 800 kN

questions.onCorrect: The projected area is 200 x 100 = 20,000 mm2, and 40 MPa on it gives 800,000 N, which is 800 kN, so the 1,000 kN press has a margin of 200 kN for the lid.

misconceptions.feedback: The clamp has to resist the pressure over the projected area only, the area seen along the direction in which the mould opens. The side walls run along that direction and do not push the two halves apart.
That is a slip of units. A pressure of 1 MPa is 1 N per mm2, so 40 x 20,000 is 800,000 N, which is 800 kN and below the 1,000 kN of the press.

choices.label: No. The whole cavity surface of 38,000 mm2 counts, so the force needed is 1,520 kN
No. The force is 40 MPa x 20,000 mm2 = 800,000 kN, which is far above 1,000 kN
Yes. The projected area is 20,000 mm2, so the clamp force needed is 800 kN

questions.prompt: Tooling for a mould costs 20,000 dollars. A moulded part then costs 1.50 each, and a printed part costs 12 each with no tooling. For 1000 parts, which route has the lower total cost?
hints: Add the tooling to the moulded total before comparing.
Moulded total: 20,000 + 1.50 x 1000. Printed total: 12 x 1000.

acceptedIdeas: Printing, because the tooling has not yet paid back.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Printing, because the tooling has not yet paid back.

questions.onCorrect: At 1000 parts the tooling has not yet paid back, and printing is cheaper by 9,500 dollars.

misconceptions.feedback: The moulded total is 20,000 + 1.50 x 1000 = 21,500 dollars, because the tooling has to be paid for as well.
Only printing has a flat cost per part. Moulding has a large cost paid at the start.

choices.label: Moulding, because the cost per part is lower.
Printing, because the tooling has not yet paid back.
They cost the same, as the cost per part is flat.

questions.prompt: In the worked example the tooling cost of 15,000 dollars is divided by the saving per part, 7.50 dollars, and not by the moulded cost of 2.40 or the printed cost of 9.90. Why?
hints: Ask what the mould buys: each moulded part costs less than a printed one, by how much?
The tooling is paid back when the savings on the parts made add up to its cost.

acceptedIdeas: Each moulded part saves that much against printing, and the savings repay the mould
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each moulded part saves that much against printing, and the savings repay the mould

questions.onCorrect: Each moulded part costs 7.50 dollars less than a printed one, and the mould pays for itself when those savings reach 15,000 dollars, which takes 2,000 parts.

misconceptions.feedback: The tooling is the price of the mould itself. The moulded cost of 2.40 is paid again on every part, on top of the mould.
Dividing by 9.90 would give 1,515 parts, and at that volume the savings add up to only 11,363 dollars, so the mould has not paid for itself. The saving of 7.50 per part is what adds up to 15,000.

choices.label: The moulded cost is already included in the 15,000 dollars of tooling for the mould
Each moulded part saves that much against printing, and the savings repay the mould
Dividing by the larger of the two costs gives the safer answer for a quotation

questions.prompt: Tooling costs 45,000 dollars. A moulded part costs 0.80 and a printed part costs 5.80. At how many parts does moulding break even?
hints: The saving per part is the printed cost less the moulded cost.
Break-even is the tooling cost divided by that saving.
The answer is a whole number of thousands.
questions.onCorrect: Past 9000 parts every extra part moulded rather than printed saves 5.00 dollars.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 5.80, the printed cost. Divide by the saving per part, 5.00.
That divides by 0.80, the moulded cost. Divide by the saving per part.

questions.prompt: In the first example the mould cost 20,000 dollars, moulded parts cost 1.50 and printed parts 12, and break-even is 1905 parts. The mould turns out to cost 40,000 dollars, with the part costs unchanged. What is the new break-even volume, in parts to the nearest whole part?
hints: The saving per part is still 10.50 dollars.
Divide the new tooling cost by the saving.
Doubling the tooling doubles the break-even.
questions.onCorrect: Break-even is proportional to the tooling cost, so a mould that costs twice as much needs twice the volume.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the earlier break-even, for the cheaper mould. The tooling cost has doubled.
That divides by 12, the printed cost. Divide by the saving per part, 10.50.

questions.prompt: A moulded box with straight vertical walls comes out of the mould with scratches on its two long side walls, and sometimes it sticks and has to be levered out. Those walls run along the direction in which the mould opens, and they have no taper. What change fixes it?
hints: A wall that runs exactly along the direction of opening rubs against the mould over its whole height as the part comes out.
What small change to the shape of the wall would let it move away from the mould as soon as it starts to move?

acceptedIdeas: Give those walls a draft of a degree or two, so that the part clears the mould as it moves
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Give those walls a draft of a degree or two, so that the part clears the mould as it moves

questions.onCorrect: A draft of 0.5 to 2 degrees tapers the walls so that the part clears the mould as soon as it moves, and the deeper the cavity, the more draft is needed.

misconceptions.feedback: More pressure presses the plastic harder against the walls, which makes the sticking worse, and it raises the clamp force that the mould needs.
A thicker wall cools more slowly and invites sink marks, and it does nothing to stop a vertical wall rubbing along the mould as the part comes out.

choices.label: Give those walls a draft of a degree or two, so that the part clears the mould as it moves
Raise the cavity pressure so that the plastic is pressed harder against the walls
Make the walls thicker so that they are stiffer as the part is pulled out

questions.prompt: A pocket in a moulded part is 100.0 mm wide at its opening and 40 mm deep, with a draft of 1 degree on each of its two long walls. A rigid insert 99.0 mm wide has to sit flat on the floor of the pocket. Does it fit?
hints: A wall with draft leans in by height x tan(draft angle) over its height.
Count the walls that have draft, and take the narrowing at the floor from the width at the opening.

acceptedIdeas: No. Both walls lean in, so the floor is only 98.6 mm wide
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No. Both walls lean in, so the floor is only 98.6 mm wide

questions.onCorrect: Each wall moves in by 40 x tan(1 degree) = 0.70 mm, so the floor is 100.0 - 1.40 = 98.6 mm wide and a 99.0 mm insert cannot sit flat. The drawing has to allow for the draft.

misconceptions.feedback: Both long walls have draft, and each moves in by 40 x tan(1 degree) = 0.70 mm over the depth of the pocket. The floor is 100.0 - 1.4 = 98.6 mm wide.
Draft tapers the walls over their whole height, so the pocket narrows towards its floor, and the floor is where the walls end up closest together.

choices.label: Yes. Draft only changes the top of the pocket, so the floor stays 100.0 mm wide
No. Both walls lean in, so the floor is only 98.6 mm wide
Yes. Only one wall leans in, so the floor is 99.3 mm wide

questions.prompt: A moulded bracket has a solid boss 12 mm thick on its back, in a part whose walls are 3 mm thick. A shallow dimple appears on the front face over the boss. What is the cause, and what is the usual fix?
hints: A thick section cools more slowly than a thin one, by the same reasoning that gave a freezing time depending on the square of V / A.
What does the plastic do as the last, thickest region cools and shrinks, with the surface already set?

acceptedIdeas: The thick boss cools last and shrinks late, pulling the surface in; hollow it out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The thick boss cools last and shrinks late, pulling the surface in; hollow it out

questions.onCorrect: The boss cools more slowly than the thin walls and shrinks after the front surface has set, which pulls a dimple into it. Designers hollow out thick regions and use ribs, so that every section cools at about the same rate.

misconceptions.feedback: Draft lets a part leave the mould and has no effect on how a thick section shrinks as it cools. A dimple over a thick section is a sink mark.
A dimple shows plastic that shrank late in the thickest section after the surface had set, and the clamp force does not change how a thick section cools.

choices.label: The boss has too little draft on its sides, so draft should be added to the boss
The cavity pressure was too high at the boss, so the clamp force should be lowered
The thick boss cools last and shrinks late, pulling the surface in; hollow it out

questions.prompt: A part is printed at 8.00 dollars each. An injection moulder quotes 24,000 dollars for the mould and 1.20 dollars for each part. At how many parts does the mould pay for itself, to the nearest whole part?
hints: Moulding saves a fixed amount on every part compared with printing. How much?
The mould is paid back when the savings add up to its cost.
Divide the cost of the mould by the saving per part.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The saving is 8.00 - 1.20 = 6.80 dollars per part, and 24,000 / 6.80 = 3,529 parts.

questions.onCorrect: Below about 3,500 parts printing is cheaper in total, and above it the mould has paid for itself.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the cost of the mould by the printed cost, 8.00. Each moulded part saves 6.80 dollars against printing, and that is the figure to divide by.
That divides the cost of the mould by the moulded cost, 1.20. The mould is paid back by what each moulded part saves against printing, 6.80 dollars.

questions.prompt: A complex part is needed in a run of 200. A mould would cost 30,000 dollars, and the part costs 12 to print. Which process fits best?
hints: Compare 200 parts with the break-even volume, which is in the thousands for a mould this dear.
Spread the cost of the mould over the 200 parts, then compare what that adds to each part with the cost of printing one.

acceptedIdeas: 3D printing, because no tooling is needed.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 3D printing, because no tooling is needed.

questions.onCorrect: Moulding has a high cost paid up front and wins only above the break-even volume.

misconceptions.feedback: The lowest cost per part is reached only when the tooling is spread over many parts. At 200 parts the tooling dominates.
A long mould life does not help when only 200 parts are wanted, since the tooling is paid for in full.
No process is always the cheapest, and it depends on the volume and the shape.

choices.label: Machining from solid, because it is always the cheapest.
Injection moulding, because moulds last for years.
Injection moulding, because it has the lowest cost per part.
3D printing, because no tooling is needed.

questions.prompt: A drawing allows a shaft diameter of 25.00 plus or minus 0.06 mm. The lathe's mean is on target and its standard deviation is 0.015 mm. How far from the mean are the limits, and what does that mean for the parts?
hints: Find the distance from the mean to a limit, then count how many standard deviations of 0.015 mm fit into it.
About 99.73 percent of the parts lie within 3 sigma of the mean.

acceptedIdeas: Each limit is 4 standard deviations out, well beyond 3 sigma, so very few parts fail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each limit is 4 standard deviations out, well beyond 3 sigma, so very few parts fail

questions.onCorrect: The limits are 0.06 / 0.015 = 4 standard deviations from the mean. Almost every part lies within 3 sigma, and about 32 parts in a million fall beyond 4 sigma on one side.

misconceptions.feedback: The 0.06 is a distance in mm. Divided by the standard deviation of 0.015 mm it comes to 4 standard deviations, which is a long way out.
Two standard deviations would be 0.03 mm. The limits are 0.06 mm from the mean, which is 4 times 0.015 mm.

choices.label: Each limit is 4 standard deviations out, well beyond 3 sigma, so very few parts fail
Each limit is 2 standard deviations out, so about 5 percent of the parts will fail
Each limit is 0.06 standard deviations out, so a large share of all the parts will fail

questions.prompt: The worked example compares the tolerance range of 0.20 mm with 6 x sigma and not with sigma alone. What does the 6 sigma stand for?
hints: About 99.73 percent of the parts lie within 3 sigma of the mean. How wide is the range from 3 sigma below to 3 sigma above?
Cp compares two widths, so the spread of the process has to be a width too.

acceptedIdeas: The width of the range that holds about 99.73 percent of the parts, 3 sigma each side
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The width of the range that holds about 99.73 percent of the parts, 3 sigma each side

questions.onCorrect: The range from 3 sigma below the mean to 3 sigma above holds about 99.73 percent of the parts, and it is 6 sigma wide. Here that is 0.18 mm, which the tolerance range of 0.20 mm only just covers.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a count of parts. The 6 sigma here is a width in mm, the spread of the process, and it is compared with the width of the tolerance.
That distance is what Cpk uses, divided by 3 sigma. Cp compares the full width of the tolerance with the full spread of the process.

choices.label: The number of parts per million that fall outside the specification limits of the part
The width of the range that holds about 99.73 percent of the parts, 3 sigma each side
The distance from the mean to the nearer of the two specification limits of a part

questions.prompt: A process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm, and the tolerance on the part is plus or minus 0.03 mm. What is Cp, to two decimal places?
hints: Cp compares the width of the tolerance range with the spread of the process.
The tolerance range runs from the lower limit to the upper limit, which is twice the half-tolerance. The spread of the process is 6 sigma.
Divide the tolerance range by the spread.
questions.onCorrect: A Cp of 1.0 means the 6 sigma spread of the process exactly fills the tolerance, so it has no margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the tolerance range by 12 sigma. Cp uses 6 sigma.
That divides the half-tolerance, 0.03 mm, by sigma. Cp divides the whole tolerance range by 6 sigma.

questions.prompt: A process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm and limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm, so its Cp is 1.67, but its mean has drifted to 25.04 mm. What do you expect?
hints: How many standard deviations are there between the mean and the upper limit?
About 16 percent of a normal distribution lies more than 1 standard deviation above the mean.

acceptedIdeas: About one part in six is above the upper limit.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About one part in six is above the upper limit.

questions.onCorrect: Cp compares the spread with the tolerance range and ignores centring, so a capable process can still make bad parts.

misconceptions.feedback: Cp ignores where the mean sits. With the mean at 25.04 the upper limit is only 1 standard deviation away.
Half of the parts would be above the mean, 25.04, but the limit is 25.05, which is above that.

choices.label: About half of the parts are outside the limits.
Almost every part is within the limits, because Cp is well above 1.
About one part in six is above the upper limit.

questions.prompt: A process has mean 24.985 mm, standard deviation 0.01 mm and limits 24.95 and 25.05 mm. Cpk = (distance to the nearer limit) / (3 sigma). What is Cpk, to two decimal places?
hints: Compare the distances to the two limits and take the smaller.
3 sigma = 0.03 mm.
Divide the nearer distance by 3 sigma.
questions.onCorrect: This process has drifted low, so the lower limit is the nearer one, and Cpk is about 1.17 against a Cp of 1.67.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the farther limit, the upper one at 0.065 mm. Cpk uses the nearer limit.
That divides by 9 sigma. Cpk divides by 3 sigma.

questions.prompt: A shaft has limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm, and the customer asks for a Cpk of at least 1.33. For each of these processes, what should be done?
hints: Work out Cp and Cpk for each process. Cp says whether the spread would fit if the mean were in the middle.
If Cp is high enough and Cpk is not, the mean is the problem. If Cp itself is too low, the spread is.
questions.onCorrect: Recentring recovers all of the capability that a narrow spread allows, but a spread that is too wide for the tolerance can only be cured by narrowing it.

items.label: Mean 25.030 mm, sigma 0.008 mm
items.explanation: Cp is 2.08 but Cpk is only 0.83. The spread is narrow enough, and the mean sits 0.02 mm from the upper limit.

items.label: Mean 25.040 mm, sigma 0.005 mm
items.explanation: Cp is 3.33 but Cpk is only 0.67. A very narrow spread is aimed too close to the upper limit.

items.label: Mean 25.000 mm, sigma 0.025 mm
items.explanation: The process is centred, so Cpk equals Cp at 0.67, and moving the mean cannot help. The spread has to shrink.

items.label: Mean 25.010 mm, sigma 0.030 mm
items.explanation: Cp is only 0.56, so even a perfectly centred process would fall short. The spread is too wide.

items.label: Mean 24.995 mm, sigma 0.010 mm
items.explanation: Cp is 1.67 and Cpk is 1.50, which is above 1.33.

items.label: Mean 25.000 mm, sigma 0.012 mm
items.explanation: The process is centred, so Cpk equals Cp at 1.39, which is above 1.33.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first two need recentring, the next two need a narrower spread, and the last two already meet 1.33.

questions.prompt: A lathe makes a shaft with limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm. Its standard deviation is 0.008 mm, and its mean has drifted to 25.03 mm. The shop can recentre the process at no cost, or buy a new lathe that halves the standard deviation but would also run at 25.03 mm. Which gives the higher Cpk?
hints: Work out the present Cpk first, from the distance to the nearer limit.
Then work out Cpk with the mean at 25.00 mm, and Cpk for sigma 0.004 mm with the mean still at 25.03 mm.

acceptedIdeas: Recentring, which gives a Cpk of 2.08 against 1.67 for the new lathe
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Recentring, which gives a Cpk of 2.08 against 1.67 for the new lathe

questions.onCorrect: The present Cpk is 0.02 / 0.024 = 0.83. Recentring gives 0.05 / 0.024 = 2.08, and the new lathe at the drifted mean gives 0.02 / 0.012 = 1.67, so the cheaper fix is also the better one.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving the spread does double the Cpk, from 0.83 to 1.67. But recentring the present lathe gives 2.08, because it lets the whole tolerance range work for the process.

choices.label: Recentring, which gives a Cpk of 2.08 against 1.67 for the new lathe
Both give the same Cpk, because Cpk always equals Cp
The new lathe, because halving the spread doubles Cpk from 0.83 to 1.67

questions.prompt: Two shifts machine the same shaft, with limits of 24.95 and 25.05 mm. The day shift has a mean of 25.012 mm and a standard deviation of 0.010 mm. The night shift has a mean of 24.999 mm and a standard deviation of 0.014 mm. Which shift has the higher Cpk?
hints: For each shift, find the distance from the mean to the nearer limit, and divide it by 3 sigma.
Both shifts are close to centred, so the spread matters a good deal. Check each result against the shift's own Cp.

acceptedIdeas: The day shift, at 1.27 against 1.17, because its narrower spread outweighs its drift
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The day shift, at 1.27 against 1.17, because its narrower spread outweighs its drift

questions.onCorrect: The day shift has Cpk = 0.038 / 0.030 = 1.27 and the night shift has 0.049 / 0.042 = 1.17. Neither reaches 1.33, but the day shift is closer, and a small drift costs less than a wider spread.

misconceptions.feedback: The night mean is nearly centred, but its spread is wider, so its Cp is only 1.19 and its Cpk cannot exceed that. It comes to 1.17.
Cpk equals Cp only when the mean is at the middle of the tolerance. The day mean is 0.012 mm off centre, so its Cpk is 1.27, below its Cp.

choices.label: The day shift, because its Cp of 1.67 is the higher and its Cpk equals that Cp
The night shift, because its mean is almost exactly on target, which makes Cpk higher
The day shift, at 1.27 against 1.17, because its narrower spread outweighs its drift

questions.prompt: A shaft has limits of 9.96 and 10.04 mm. The process has a standard deviation of 0.01 mm and its mean is at 10.02 mm. What is Cpk, to two decimal places?
hints: Find which limit is nearer: 10.04 - 10.02 or 10.02 - 9.96.
The nearer distance is 0.02 mm.
Divide by 3 sigma = 0.03 mm.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The upper limit is the nearer, 0.02 mm away: Cpk = 0.02 / (3 x 0.01) = 0.67.

questions.onCorrect: A Cpk below 1 means the nearer limit is under 3 standard deviations from the mean, and many parts will be out of limits.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the farther limit, the lower one at 0.06 mm. Cpk uses the nearer limit.
That is the Cp, which ignores the shift of the mean.

questions.prompt: A process has Cp = 1.5 and Cpk = 0.5. What does this say about it?
hints: Compare Cp, which ignores centring, with Cpk, which does not.
Ask which of the two indices would change if you moved the mean without changing the spread.

acceptedIdeas: Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.

questions.onCorrect: Recentring the mean would bring Cpk up towards the Cp of 1.5, without any change to the spread.

misconceptions.feedback: A Cp of 1.5 means the spread fits well within the tolerance range. The low Cpk comes from the position of the mean.
Cpk of 0.5 means the nearer limit is only 1.5 standard deviations from the mean, so a good many parts fall outside.
Measuring more parts only gives a better estimate of Cpk. The process has to be centred to change it.

choices.label: Measuring more parts will raise the Cpk to match the Cp.
Its spread is too wide for the tolerance, so many parts miss.
It is making no parts out of limits, as Cp is above 1.
Its spread is small enough, but its mean is off centre.

questions.prompt:
A designer wants the lightest square-section beam of a given length and a given stiffness. E is in GPa and density in g/cm3.

`Steel                  210   7.85`
`Titanium               116   4.50`
`Aluminium               70   2.70`
`Glass-fibre composite   40   1.90`
`Nylon                    3   1.14`

Which material gives the lightest beam?
hints: For a stiff, light beam the materials are ranked by one index, and not by E or density alone.
Work out the square root of E divided by the density for each row, and pick the largest.

acceptedIdeas: The glass-fibre composite, which has the highest value of sqrt(E) / density
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The glass-fibre composite, which has the highest value of sqrt(E) / density

questions.onCorrect: The values of sqrt(E) / density are 1.85 for steel, 2.39 for titanium, 3.10 for aluminium, 3.33 for the composite and 1.52 for nylon. The composite has the best, so its beam is the lightest for the same stiffness.

misconceptions.feedback: E / density is the index for a tie rod in tension. A beam in bending uses sqrt(E) / density, and steel's value of 1.85 is among the lowest here.
Nylon's E is only 3 GPa, so a beam of it needs a far larger section to be as stiff. Its value of sqrt(E) / density is 1.52, the lowest of the five.
Aluminium's 3.10 is the best of the metals but it is below the composite's 3.33, and the question is open to every material in the table.

choices.label: Nylon, which has the lowest density and so should give the lightest beam
Steel, which has the highest value of E / density and the highest stiffness
Aluminium, because it is the lightest of the three metals in the table
The glass-fibre composite, which has the highest value of sqrt(E) / density

questions.prompt: A beam of aluminium is made as stiff as a steel beam of the same length and a similar shape. Aluminium is about a third as dense as steel and about a third as stiff. Roughly how does the mass of the aluminium beam compare with the steel one?
hints: A less stiff material needs a larger section to bend as little.
Ask whether the section has to grow as much as the density falls.

acceptedIdeas: It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.

questions.onCorrect: The aluminium beam has about 0.60 of the steel beam's mass, a saving of 40 percent where density alone would suggest 66 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: The section is larger, about 1.73 times the area, but each cubic centimetre weighs only about a third as much, so the beam still comes out lighter.
A third of the mass would follow if the two beams were the same size, but the aluminium beam needs a larger section to be as stiff, so it weighs more than a third of the steel one.
A beam's stiffness grows with the fourth power of its side, so a modest increase in section makes up for the lower stiffness and the mass grows by less than the density falls.

choices.label: It is about a third of the mass, in proportion to the density.
It is lighter, but well over a third of the mass.
It is heavier, because it needs a larger section.
It is about the same, because the lower density and the lower stiffness cancel out.

questions.prompt: In the worked example E goes under a square root in the index for a stiff, light beam. Why is the index sqrt(E) / density and not E / density?
hints: The stiffness of a square beam goes as E times the fourth power of its side. How does the side needed change when E falls?
The mass is the density times the area, and the area is the side squared.

acceptedIdeas: The side needed goes as the fourth root of 1 / E, and mass goes as the side squared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The side needed goes as the fourth root of 1 / E, and mass goes as the side squared

questions.onCorrect: A fixed stiffness needs a side proportional to 1 / E^(1/4), and the mass is the density times the side squared, which is proportional to density / sqrt(E).

misconceptions.feedback: The root comes from the shape of the beam and has nothing to do with the unit. A change of unit would multiply every index by the same factor and leave the ranking alone.
The mass is proportional to the density and not to its square. It is the side of the beam that is squared, in the area, and the side depends on the fourth root of E.

choices.label: The side needed goes as the fourth root of 1 / E, and mass goes as the side squared
E is measured in GPa, a large unit, so taking a root brings it to a convenient size
Density is squared in the formula for the mass, so E has to be rooted to balance it

questions.prompt: Magnesium has E = 45 GPa and density 1.74 g/cm3. What is its performance index for a stiff, light beam, to two decimal places?
hints: The index is the square root of E divided by the density.
The square root of 45 is 6.708.
The answer is between 3 and 4.
questions.onCorrect: At 3.86 magnesium beats aluminium by about a quarter, though it stays far behind the carbon-fibre composite and the wood.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides E by density without taking the square root of E.
That is the square root of E alone. Divide it by the density.

questions.prompt: A designer replaces a steel beam, and separately a steel tie rod, with aluminium of the same length and the same stiffness, to save mass. Steel has E = 210 GPa and density 7.85 g/cm3, and aluminium has E = 70 GPa and density 2.70 g/cm3. What happens to the two masses?
hints: A beam in bending is ranked by sqrt(E) / density, and a tie rod in tension by E / density.
Work out the mass of each aluminium part as a fraction of the steel one: the ratio of the two indices, steel over aluminium.

acceptedIdeas: The beam is about 40 percent lighter, and the tie rod about the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The beam is about 40 percent lighter, and the tie rod about the same

questions.onCorrect: For the beam the ratio is 1.85 / 3.10 = 0.60, which is a saving of 40 percent. For the tie rod it is (2.70 / 70) / (7.85 / 210) = 1.03, so the aluminium rod weighs slightly more than the steel one.

misconceptions.feedback: Aluminium is also about a third as stiff, so it needs a larger section. The beam comes out at 0.60 of the steel mass, and the tie rod at 1.03.
Different jobs have different indices: sqrt(E) / density for the beam and E / density for the tie rod. The beam saves 40 percent and the tie rod saves nothing.
That is reversed. Aluminium saves 40 percent in a beam, at 0.60 of the steel mass, and nothing in a tie rod, at 1.03 of it.

choices.label: Both are about 40 percent lighter, because the same index applies to each
The tie rod is about 40 percent lighter, and the beam about the same
Both are about 66 percent lighter, because aluminium is about a third as dense
The beam is about 40 percent lighter, and the tie rod about the same

questions.prompt: A single complex metal prototype is wanted. Which process fits best?
hints: With only one part, any tooling cost falls entirely on that part.
Check which of the three processes need dies or moulds made before the first part, and what that costs when you make one part.

acceptedIdeas: Metal 3D printing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Metal 3D printing

questions.onCorrect: Additive manufacturing has no tooling, so cost per part is flat, and it can make shapes that no mould could release.

misconceptions.feedback: A die costs tens of thousands of dollars, which for a single part is far more than printing.
Closed-die forging needs a pair of dies shaped for the part, so for one prototype their cost would outweigh everything else.

choices.label: Metal 3D printing
Die casting
Forging in closed dies

questions.prompt: A steel beam (E = 210 GPa, density 7.85 g/cm3) is to be replaced by a titanium beam (E = 116 GPa, density 4.5 g/cm3) of the same length, the same square shape and the same stiffness. By what percentage is the titanium beam lighter, to the nearest percent?
hints: For a stiff beam of fixed shape, the mass goes as the density divided by the square root of E.
Work out sqrt(E) / density for each metal. The ratio of the masses is the steel index over the titanium index.
Take the mass ratio away from 1 and express the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The indices are 1.85 for steel and 2.39 for titanium, so the titanium beam has 1.85 / 2.39 = 0.77 of the mass, a saving of 23 percent.

questions.onCorrect: Titanium saves about a quarter of the mass, much less than the 43 percent that its lower density suggests on its own, because it is also less stiff and needs a larger section.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the densities alone, 4.5 against 7.85. Titanium is also less stiff than steel, so the beam needs a larger section, and the saving is smaller.
That is the mass of the titanium beam as a percentage of the steel beam's. The question asks for how much lighter it is, which is 100 minus that.

questions.prompt: A beam on a boat dock must be as light as possible for a given stiffness. It will stay wet, and the budget rules out carbon fibre. Ranked by sqrt(E) / density, the candidates are carbon-fibre composite 6.45, pine 6.32, aluminium 3.10 and steel 1.85. Which should be chosen?
hints: The usual method is to rank by the index, then to screen the leading materials against the other limits.
Cross out each leading material that fails a limit stated in the question, and take the best of what is left.

acceptedIdeas: Aluminium, the best index among the materials that pass both limits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Aluminium, the best index among the materials that pass both limits

questions.onCorrect: Carbon fibre fails on cost and pine fails in wet conditions, and of the two that remain, aluminium at 3.10 has a better index than steel at 1.85.

misconceptions.feedback: The index ranks the mass only. The budget rules carbon fibre out, so it has to be screened out before the best of the rest is taken.
Pine ranks second, but wood suffers in wet conditions, so it fails the screen on a dock that stays wet.
Steel ranks last on the index, at 1.85, which gives the heaviest beam for the stiffness. Aluminium has the better index and passes both limits.

choices.label: Steel, because it does not rot as pine does in wet conditions
Carbon-fibre composite, because it has the highest index of the four
Aluminium, the best index among the materials that pass both limits
Pine, because its index is almost as high as the composite's

questions.prompt: About 100,000 thin-walled aluminium housings with a complex shape are needed every year. Which process fits?
hints: At this volume the tooling cost is shared among a great many parts.
Think about which processes make thousands of identical parts cheaply once the tooling exists, and which keep a high cost per part however many you make.

acceptedIdeas: Die casting
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Die casting

questions.onCorrect: Die casting pays for a steel die once and then makes each housing cheaply, which suits aluminium at high volume.

misconceptions.feedback: Printing has a flat cost per part that is far higher than a cast part at this volume.
Machining each housing would waste most of the material and take a long time per part.
Sand casting has a rougher surface and looser tolerance, and it needs a new mould for each part.

choices.label: Die casting
Sand casting
3D printing
Machining from solid

questions.prompt: Past the peak of a tensile test, a bar of original area 80 mm2 carries a force of 28 kN, and its neck has narrowed to 60 mm2. What is the true stress at the neck, in MPa to the nearest MPa?
hints: True stress divides the force by the area the bar has at that moment.
Use the area of the neck, 60 mm2, and the force in newtons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: True stress uses the area the bar has now: 28,000 N / 60 mm2 = 466.7 MPa, which is 467 MPa.

questions.onCorrect: The true stress is 467 MPa, well above the engineering stress of 350 MPa on the same force, because the neck has much less area than A0.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the original area of 80 mm2, which gives the engineering stress. True stress uses the area of the neck.
That leaves the force in kilonewtons, so the stress is in GPa. Use newtons to get MPa.

questions.prompt: The worked example divides the extension of 10 mm by the original gauge length of 50 mm, and not by the final length of 60 mm. Why is the original length used?
hints: Think about which length is the same whatever the load on the bar.
Check each option against the numbers in the prompt, 10 mm over 50 mm and 10 mm over 60 mm.

acceptedIdeas: It is the one length known before the test, so all readings share it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is the one length known before the test, so all readings share it

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by the original length gives every bar the same fixed reference, so the elongation of a thick bar and a thin bar of the same steel can be compared.

choices.label: The final length is hard to measure after the bar has broken, so it is avoided
It is the one length known before the test, so all readings share it
Dividing by the final length would give a result above 100 percent

misconceptions.feedback: The marks can be fitted together after the break, as the first line says, so the final length is easy to find.
Here 10 / 60 is about 17 percent, far below 100, so the size of the result is not what decides the choice.

questions.prompt: Specific stiffness is E divided by the density. What does a higher value tell a designer about a material?
hints: E is stiffness, and the density tells how much each cubic centimetre weighs.
Say in words what E divided by the density compares: stiffness against what?

acceptedIdeas: It gives more stiffness for each unit of mass
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It gives more stiffness for each unit of mass

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by density asks how much stiffness each unit of mass buys, which is what a designer who wants a light part needs.

choices.label: It needs more mass for each unit of stiffness
It gives more stiffness for each unit of mass
It gives more strength for each unit of mass

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the ratio upside down: with density on the bottom, a lighter material gives a larger value.
Strength is a different property, found at yield or at the peak of the curve. E measures stiffness.

questions.prompt: Along the fibres, the fibre carries far more of the load than the matrix does. Why?
hints: Bonded parts that are pulled along their length stretch by the same amount.
Ask what the stress in each part is when the strain is equal.

acceptedIdeas: Both stretch by the same strain, so the stiffer fibre takes more stress
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both stretch by the same strain, so the stiffer fibre takes more stress

questions.onCorrect: Equal strain means the stress in each part is its modulus times that strain, so the stiffer fibre carries most of the load.

choices.label: Both carry the same stress, so the load divides equally between them
The fibre takes up more volume, so it carries more of the load
Both stretch by the same strain, so the stiffer fibre takes more stress

misconceptions.feedback: Equal stress is the case across the fibres. Along them, bonded parts must stretch by the same amount.
The fibre fraction matters, but even a small fraction of fibre carries most of the load along the fibres, because it is so much stiffer.

questions.prompt: True strain in rolling is ln(h0 / h1), with the starting thickness h0 on top. Why is the ratio written this way round?
hints: Work out h0 / h1 for a plate that goes from 30 mm to 25 mm, and compare it with 1.
Decide which thickness is larger in a rolling pass, then put it where the ratio comes out above 1.

acceptedIdeas: Thinning makes the ratio larger than 1, so the strain is positive
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thinning makes the ratio larger than 1, so the strain is positive

questions.onCorrect: Putting the larger starting thickness on top gives a ratio above 1, and so a positive true strain, for a reduction in thickness.

choices.label: A logarithm only works if the larger number is on the bottom of the ratio
Thinning makes the ratio larger than 1, so the strain is positive
The final thickness is always larger than the starting one

misconceptions.feedback: A logarithm can be taken of any positive ratio, large or small, so that is not the reason.
In rolling the plate gets thinner, so the starting thickness is the larger one.

flashcards.front: What is the highest engineering stress on a stress-strain curve called?
flashcards.back: It is the ultimate tensile strength, reached when necking begins.

acceptedIdeas: ultimate tensile strength
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ultimate tensile strength

flashcards.front: A part has to absorb as much energy as possible by deforming before it breaks. Does a higher yield strength settle the choice of material?
flashcards.back: No. The energy absorbed is the area under the whole curve, so a steel that yields lower but stretches much further can absorb more than a stronger steel that breaks at a small strain.

flashcards.front: Why does toughness differ from strength?
flashcards.back: Strength is a stress, while toughness is the area under the curve, the energy absorbed per volume before fracture.

flashcards.front: Which kind of bond lets layers of atoms slide in a metal?
flashcards.back: Metallic bonding is not tied to a pair of atoms, so layers can slide and the metal deforms.

acceptedIdeas: metallic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: metallic

flashcards.front: A designer makes a nylon rod as stiff as an aluminium one of the same length. Why does it end up much heavier?
flashcards.back: Nylon's E is about 23 times smaller, so its section has to be about 23 times larger, and even at 0.42 times the density the rod is about ten times as heavy.

flashcards.front: Why can strong bonds go with a brittle material?
flashcards.back: Strong bonds give a high stiffness, but if they resist sliding the material cannot deform plastically, so a crack grows instead.

flashcards.front: What is the defect whose movement lets a metal deform plastically?
flashcards.back: A dislocation moves a row at a time, so far less stress is needed than for sliding a whole plane.

acceptedIdeas: dislocation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dislocation

flashcards.front: Which of the three ways of strengthening a metal costs conductivity, and which costs ductility?
flashcards.back: Alloying costs conductivity and work hardening costs ductility, while finer grains usually keep toughness.

flashcards.front: Why does work hardening raise strength but lower ductility?
flashcards.back: Cold work multiplies dislocations that tangle and block each other, which makes slip harder and leaves less capacity to deform further.

flashcards.front: Which structure forms when steel is quenched?
flashcards.back: Fast cooling traps carbon in the iron lattice as martensite, which is very hard and brittle.

acceptedIdeas: martensite
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: martensite

flashcards.front: A 0.40 percent carbon steel cooled slowly: fraction of pearlite, to three decimal places?
Why does tempering follow quenching?
flashcards.back: Quenched martensite is hard but brittle, and reheating lets some carbon leave it, which gives up a little hardness for much more toughness.

flashcards.front: A polymer part has to stay stiff in a place that reaches 60 C. What do you check about the polymer's glass transition temperature?
flashcards.back: Tg must lie above 60 C. Below Tg the chains are frozen and the polymer is stiff, and above it the stiffness drops by a factor of a hundred or more.

flashcards.front: Stiffness along the fibres: Ef = 100 GPa, Em = 4 GPa, 50 percent fibre?
Why is a composite so much stiffer along its fibres than across them?
flashcards.back: Along the fibres the stiff fibres share the strain and carry most of the load, but across them the load passes through the soft matrix in series.

flashcards.front: What property of a material gives the stress intensity at which a crack runs?
flashcards.back: Fracture toughness K_IC, in MPa times the square root of metres, is the stress intensity at which a crack grows.

acceptedIdeas: fracture toughness
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fracture toughness

flashcards.front: A stronger steel is offered for a part that is inspected for cracks. What has to be checked besides its yield strength?
flashcards.back: Its fracture toughness. The critical crack length, (K_IC / stress)^2 / pi, can be smaller in a stronger steel, so inspection has to find shorter cracks.

flashcards.front: Why can a small crack be dangerous in a strong material?
flashcards.back: Stress piles up at the crack tip, and a strong material with low toughness can have a critical stress at the tip far below its yield strength.

flashcards.front: Two metals are joined in a wet joint. Which one loses metal, and how can you tell from their electrode potentials?
flashcards.back: The metal with the more negative standard electrode potential, the more active one, becomes the anode and loses metal. The other metal is the cathode and is protected.

flashcards.front: Iron (M = 55.85, n = 2) corrodes at 0.01 A for 1000 s. Grams lost, to three decimal places?
flashcards.back: m = 0.01 x 1000 x 55.85 / (2 x 96485) = 0.0029 g, which is 0.003 g to three decimal places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: m = 0.01 x 1000 x 55.85 / (2 x 96485) = 0.0029 g, which is 0.003 g to three decimal places.

flashcards.front: Why does a scratched coating of zinc still protect steel but a scratched coating of paint may not?
flashcards.back: Zinc is the more active metal, so it is the anode and corrodes in the steel's place, but paint is only a barrier and the exposed steel rusts beneath it.

flashcards.front: A casting section is made three times thicker, so V / A triples. By what factor does the freezing time change?
flashcards.back: Time goes as (V / A)^2, so it changes by 3 squared, which is 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Time goes as (V / A)^2, so it changes by 3 squared, which is 9.

flashcards.front: Why is a pattern made larger than the casting it will make?
flashcards.back: The solid casting shrinks as it cools to room temperature, so the pattern is the casting length divided by (1 - s), where s is the fraction that the metal shrinks.

flashcards.front: Why must the riser freeze after the casting?
flashcards.back: The riser must stay liquid long enough to feed the casting as it shrinks, so the shrinkage hole ends up in the riser.

flashcards.front: Rolling from 12 mm to 8 mm: true strain to three decimal places?
A bent high-strength sheet opens out when the tool lifts. Why does it happen, and what does the operator change?
flashcards.back: Part of the strain in the bend was elastic and recovers when the load is removed, and a higher-strength sheet stores more of it. The operator bends slightly past the target angle.

flashcards.front: Why does forging need more force as it proceeds?
flashcards.back: The volume is constant, so as the billet gets shorter its contact area grows, and force is flow stress times area.

flashcards.front: Material removal rate: v = 100 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev, d = 1 mm. In cm3/min?
Taylor, n = 0.25: speed ratio 0.9. Factor in tool life, two decimals?
Why is faster cutting not always cheaper per part?
flashcards.back: Tool life falls much faster than speed rises, so the cost of worn tools and tool changes can outweigh the time saved.

flashcards.front: To find the clamp force of an injection moulded part, which area do you use, and why?
flashcards.back: The projected area, seen along the direction in which the mould opens, because the cavity pressure pushes the halves apart over that area only. The walls that run along the direction of opening do not push them apart.

flashcards.front: Break-even: tooling 10,000, moulded 1.00, printed 6.00. How many parts?
Why does the cost per part fall as the run gets longer when moulding?
flashcards.back: The tooling cost is fixed, so it is shared among more parts, while the moulded cost per part stays the same.

flashcards.front: A process has a Cp of 1.6 and a Cpk of 0.7. Does it need a more precise machine?
flashcards.back: No. Cp shows that the spread fits inside the tolerance, and the low Cpk shows that the mean is off centre. Recentring the process raises Cpk towards Cp without any change to the spread.

flashcards.front: A process has a standard deviation of 0.02 mm and a tolerance range of 0.12 mm. Cp?
Why can a process with Cp above 1 still make parts out of tolerance?
flashcards.back: Cp ignores the mean, so a process that is off centre can have a nearer limit that is only a little way from the mean and so make many bad parts.

flashcards.front: Which index ranks materials for a stiff, light tie rod, and which for a stiff, light beam?
flashcards.back: A tie rod is ranked by E divided by density and a beam by the square root of E divided by density, so the best material depends on the job.

flashcards.front: Which kind of process suits a few thousand or more parts of a plastic, once its tooling has been paid for?
flashcards.back: Injection moulding has high tooling cost and low cost per part, so it suits large volumes.

acceptedIdeas: injection moulding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: injection moulding

flashcards.front: Why should material and process be chosen together?
flashcards.back: The process limits which materials and shapes are possible, and the material limits which processes can be used, so each choice changes the other.
